Following Donald Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two respects — a shift from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and a shift from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. Notably, risks facing emerging market economies have intensified amid the faster pace of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and potential US trade protectionist measures. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank rates rose in tandem with US dollar interbank rates. Nonetheless, liquidity conditions remained favourable, and overall loan growth picked up further in the second half of 2016. Following the introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed signs of correction, but has since rebounded. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the risk of a faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate increases and, more broadly, the implications of US policy uncertainty — in particular the risk of significant capital outflows and the potential impact on local interest rates.  Following Donald Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only was the election outcome a surprise to the market, but the subsequent market reaction was also unexpected. In particular, expectations that Trump's proposed tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending and deregulation would boost US economic growth drove global equity markets higher. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two respects — a shift from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and a shift from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. However, the Trump tax cuts that markets are anticipating may not deliver the expected stimulus to US economic growth. In particular, given that US economic activity is already operating close to its potential, fiscal stimulus may only provide a modest cyclical boost to US growth, while heightening upside risks to US inflation. Although it remains to be seen whether the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening as a result, long-term bond yields have risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks.  Meanwhile, the rise of trade protectionism would create a "lose-lose" outcome for the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would cause market distortions that are harmful to overall welfare, impede global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the European economy, where recovery remains fragile. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows due to a faster pace of US rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation has risen. This could weigh on economic growth and heighten the risk of sudden and large-scale capital outflows. Indeed, with expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion under the Trump administration and concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices, markets have repriced inflation risks, leading to broadly significant increases in long-term bond yields across both advanced economies and many emerging market economies.  Special Topic 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US rate hike expectations on sovereign bond markets in 26 selected economies. The findings show that the influence of the US Treasury bond market on sovereign bond markets has deepened since the 2013 "taper tantrum," and that US rate hikes and tightening financial conditions would have significant impacts on both advanced economies and emerging market economies.  In East Asia, economic growth edged up slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by a recovery in exports, but market volatility — including currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields — triggered by concerns about possible policy changes under the new US administration only gradually stabilised at the start of this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces have increased. US rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and heightened financial market volatility could lead to a tightening of financial conditions. At the same time, possible US protectionist policies could affect regional economies, although the actual impact remains unclear at this stage.  On the Chinese Mainland, overall economic growth edged up modestly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust infrastructure investment growth and improving private sector capital expenditure. Although there are continued signs of stabilisation in the economy, the growth outlook for the Mainland remains uncertain. In particular, if the real estate market continues to cool amid the government's determination to curb property price increases, the contribution of the real estate sector to growth this year may diminish. Meanwhile, the ongoing progress of economic structural adjustment and changes in Sino-US trade relations may add to short-term economic uncertainty. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 as the US dollar strengthened and expectations of faster US rate hikes grew, and appeared to ease somewhat in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private sector economic activity, there remain some concerns in the market about the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly in view of accelerating M1 growth alongside slowing M2 growth. Special Topic 2 (see page 24) examines whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, and Special Topic 3 (see page 27) explores the factors that may have caused the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings suggest that there is no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and that the primary reasons for M1 growth significantly outpacing M2 growth are the reduction in the opportunity cost of holding liquid money resulting from recent monetary easing, and the possibility that rising economic uncertainty has increased precautionary money demand.  Hong Kong's economic growth edged up modestly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. On the domestic side, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter boosted investment growth. On the external front, goods export growth rose in line with improved trade flows in the region, while services exports grew steadily as trade-related and transportation services recovered. As imports of goods and services grew at a faster pace, net exports continued to be a drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. As economic growth picked up, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December.  Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. The government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2–3% and 2.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric from the new US administration has added downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong's external demand. With upward pressure on the US dollar and expectations of a faster pace of US rate hikes, global financial conditions are likely to become less supportive of the real economy, and could lead to a tightening of local financial conditions, particularly if tail risks materialise. Special Topic 4 (see page 41) discusses the construction of a financial conditions index for Hong Kong to help monitor local financial conditions.  Since the second half of 2016, local inflationary pressures have remained moderate, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum edged up slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, driven mainly by food price volatility and rising housing rentals. With stable import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable.  Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, though it softened occasionally following the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. With the appreciation of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate rose further. Due to the large monetary base, Hong Kong interbank rates remained low, but have risen since October due to year-end funding demand and catching up with US dollar rate hikes. As a result, the average mortgage rate, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business, edged up to 2.07% in January 2017.  Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% in the first half. Growth was supported by stronger domestic economic activity and increased year-end financing needs from multinational corporations. Domestic loan growth edged up modestly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a slight decline in the first half. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans recorded growth of 3.2%, as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans.  Banking sector funding conditions remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down to 77.1% at end-2016, reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, while the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio declined significantly to 63.8%, driven by strong US dollar deposit growth.  With the US dollar strengthening, both the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool (comprising customer deposits and certificates of deposit outstanding) consolidated further alongside other offshore renminbi markets, and volatility in offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank rates increased significantly. Nonetheless, banks' renminbi liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi real-time gross settlement system remained at a high level. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business will likely continue to face headwinds from uncertainty surrounding renminbi exchange rate movements.  As global market conditions improved, Hong Kong's stock market ended the review period with substantial gains. Despite the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election, the market experienced only a brief setback. This was largely driven by investor optimism about fiscal stimulus measures under the Trump administration, which boosted global equity markets. While benefiting from this sentiment, the local market remained cautiously optimistic, possibly due to concerns about a faster pace of US rate hikes, challenges to the Mainland economic outlook, uncertainty over renminbi policy, and capital flow controls.  Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuations could provide support.  Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply and their spread over US Treasury bonds widened rapidly towards the end of last year, the Hong Kong dollar bond market continued to expand steadily during the review period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi bond market rebounded in the second half of 2016 following a contraction in the first half, although new bond issuance for the full year was still lower than the previous year. Looking ahead, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets would come under pressure if global investors reverse their earlier search-for-yield investment strategies. With US trade policy still uncertain and the renminbi exchange rate likely to remain volatile, the outlook for both bond markets over the next six months will continue to be clouded by significant uncertainties.  Following the government's introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed signs of correction, but has since rebounded. In light of renewed market exuberance, the government raised stamp duty to a flat rate of 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets fell in the subsequent two months. However, transaction volumes have since risen, partly reflecting developers launching more new first-hand residential projects. Property prices continued to climb to new highs, though the pace of increase has moderated.

Following the unexpected election of Donald Trump as US President, uncertainty surrounding US policy has increased. While market attention has focused on the near-term benefits of potentially large fiscal stimulus and business-friendly measures, US economic activity is already operating close to its economic potential, meaning that fiscal stimulus is likely to provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth, while further exacerbating upside risks to inflation. More importantly, risks facing emerging market economies are rising amid capital outflow pressures stemming from a faster pace of US interest rate increases and a strengthening US dollar, and potential US protectionist trade measures also threaten global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and export volumes have increased recently. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation, and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, and downside risks to growth have increased. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated modestly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved business spending in the private sector. The mainland economy has continued to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, though the ongoing progress of structural adjustment and potential changes in Sino-US trade relations may add to near-term uncertainty in the economic outlook. Given the government's resolve to curb rising property prices, a continued cooling of the property market could also reduce the real estate sector's contribution to economic growth this year. On the external front, while the renminbi remained broadly stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 as the US dollar strengthened and US interest rates rose, before appearing to ease somewhat in early 2017. Global financial markets reacted strongly to the unexpected election of Donald Trump as US President, particularly as market expectations that Trump's proposed tax reforms, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost US economic growth and inflation drove major equity markets higher (Chart 2.1). Consequently, market expectations for US inflation and US interest rate increases picked up, causing US Treasury yields to rise sharply and the US dollar to strengthen. Chart 2.1 Stock market indices of selected advanced economies. However, the Trump tax cuts that markets are anticipating may not deliver the positive impact on US economic growth that markets expect. While a shift in economic policy towards greater reliance on fiscal easing would help reduce the heavy burden on monetary easing, the appropriateness of implementing fiscal easing measures at this juncture—given the current stage of the US economic cycle—is debatable. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap has been narrowing, and the February unemployment rate of 4.7% is in line with the Federal Reserve's estimate of the natural rate of unemployment, suggesting that US economic activity is already close to its economic potential. With the US economy currently in an expansionary phase of the cycle, fiscal multipliers will be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))¹. Indeed, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital could lead to a reduction in tax revenues (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))². In any case, with spare capacity diminishing, any further measures to boost growth, even if their actual impact on growth is limited, could push up inflation. At the same time, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, and potential protectionist trade measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, could further exacerbate upside risks to US inflation. Even as risks of higher US inflation have increased, the Federal Reserve has remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and has been inclined to maintain its ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. Nevertheless, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risks. Since the US election, while market forecasts for future federal funds rates have been revised upward to near the Federal Reserve's median projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Federal Reserve's long-run projections (Chart 2.2). Accordingly, a faster pace of US interest rate increases could trigger the risk of significant market volatility. While financial market attention has focused on the near-term benefits of potentially expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures driving stronger US economic growth, longer-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further increase in US public debt. Indeed, the Trump administration may follow through on its campaign pledges to adopt protectionist trade measures. Increased trade barriers would cause market distortions that harm overall welfare, impede global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Projections of future federal funds rates: Federal Reserve versus markets. In Europe, political uncertainty remains the primary risk and headwind to the European economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the euro area has gradually improved, with real GDP growing at a moderate 1.7% year-on-year in the fourth quarter—only slightly below the 1.8% year-on-year increase in the third quarter—euro area economic activity remains only marginally above pre-global financial crisis levels relative to the stronger recovery seen in the United States (Chart 2.3). Since the UK's decision to leave the European Union last summer, markets have been concerned about the ultimate disintegration of the euro area. While the economic and political situation in Italy appears to have stabilised somewhat following the formation of a new government and the implementation of measures to rescue the banking sector, the upcoming elections in Germany and France (and potentially Italy) could become political flashpoints against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly due to heightened political uncertainty, European sovereign bond yields have continued to rise, and corporate bond spreads have widened—particularly in peripheral countries—which could create a vicious cycle detrimental to the real economy and may exert pressure on business fixed investment in the euro area. Chart 2.3 Real GDP of major advanced economies. In Japan, real GDP has been revised upward for recent quarters, with the annualised growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2016 increasing to 1.6% year-on-year—the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015—suggesting that the economic recovery is stronger than previously anticipated. However, partly due to structural issues in the labour market, wage growth has remained slow, resulting in weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the recent sharp depreciation of the yen suggests that the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation from earlier yen appreciation is beginning to abate. Together with the stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates some improvement in the near-term inflation outlook, and "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy)—although it fell to 0.1% in December—is expected to bottom out and recover. Nonetheless, growth is likely to remain sluggish in the face of persistent structural and long-term headwinds, and inflation expectations remain anchored at around 0.5%–0.6%, below the levels seen when Abenomics was launched in early 2014, leaving the risk that inflation will fail to reach the Bank of Japan's 2% medium-term target. For other countries, particularly emerging market economies, the benefits of stronger US growth through trade channels may be limited, as US imports declined following the global financial crisis and the United States may implement protectionist policies. At the same time, a faster pace of US interest rate increases and further US dollar appreciation will tighten financial conditions and amplify downside economic risks. This could weigh on growth and increase the risk of a sharp reversal of capital flows. Indeed, markets' repricing of inflation risk—driven by expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration and concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices—has caused long-term bond yields to rise significantly and broadly across both advanced economies and a number of emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of expectations of US interest rate increases on sovereign bond markets in 26 selected economies. In East Asia³, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with modest GDP growth and rising inflation across the region. Real GDP growth — In the second half of 2016, growth remained broadly stable across the region as private consumption in several regional economies held steady. Export volumes also generally recovered modestly from their 2015 lows, benefiting not only from China's stabilising growth but also from improved performance in advanced economies such as the United States and Europe. For net commodity exporters such as Malaysia and Indonesia, the recovery in commodity prices provided an additional boost. Other major exporters such as South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore also regained momentum on the back of growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — Broadly consistent with the recovery in commodity (especially oil) prices, producer price inflation has generally trended upward. While this will push up industrial costs and potentially consumer spending, consumer and investment growth could be supported by a reduction in long-term deflation risks. The acceleration in producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which producer price increases are passed through to consumer prices—a process that is uneven across economies. Consensus forecasts for the Consumer Price Index suggest that inflation in several regional economies, while still likely to remain slightly below the respective central bank targets for 2017, will rise to levels closer to those targets (Chart 2.4). With the exception of Indonesia, central banks across East Asia have broadly maintained their accommodative monetary policy stances, while Indonesia cut interest rates twice in September and October of last year to support growth. Chart 2.4 Headline CPI inflation, forecasts and central bank targets in East Asia. Despite the improvement in real economic activity, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 caused short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign exchange markets — Following the US presidential election, most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar as investors anticipated higher US inflation. However, on a trade-weighted basis, several regional currencies depreciated by less than implied by their bilateral moves against the US dollar, and some even appreciated modestly (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Post-US election spot forex depreciation against the USD and changes in nominal effective exchange rates. Bond and equity markets — Asset prices fell briefly following the US presidential election before stabilising. Sovereign bond spreads over US Treasuries widened for East Asian economies. However, as markets stabilised, yields in some regional economies declined, though they have yet to fully return to pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nonetheless, spreads have narrowed relative to pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads of 10-year sovereign bonds over US Treasuries. Portfolio investment flows — Portfolio capital flows recorded outflows from East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, though the pace was slower than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. Capital inflows resumed in the first few weeks of 2017, providing support for asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth is expected to remain broadly stable, albeit at a pace below its historical average. With uncertainty surrounding US government policies and the Federal Reserve's potential policy responses both elevated, financial markets are likely to remain volatile. A sharp rise in the US dollar and US yields could attract capital away from the region towards the United States, prompting investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets—particularly those that are already more richly valued. A tightening of financial conditions under such circumstances would also place repayment pressure on corporates with large US dollar-denominated debt. More broadly, a general rise in global interest rates would reduce fixed capital investment in the region, weighing on aggregate demand in the near term and potentially affecting potential growth over the longer term. Finally, regional exporters face the potential threat of protectionist trade policies from the new US administration. The trade deficits that the United States has run with East Asian economies have widened persistently in recent years (Chart 2.7), particularly in key export industries in the region such as electronics, electrical equipment, automobiles, clothing, and textiles. Over the past two decades, increased US imports in these sectors have resulted in a large number of job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing trade deficits and revitalising US manufacturing could pose significant risks to exporting economies in the region.

Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016, driven by faster private consumption growth and buoyant building and construction activity in the public sector. Given the increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. Inflationary pressures are projected to remain contained, supported by stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum.  Hong Kong's economic growth edged up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly above the 0.8% recorded in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Private consumption growth accelerated, partly due to improved consumer confidence and resilient labour market conditions, becoming the primary driver of GDP growth. Building and construction activity also picked up, supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport. However, overall investment expenditure's contribution to GDP growth narrowed due to weak corporate capital spending. On the external side, both merchandise exports and imports accelerated alongside rising regional trade flows (Chart 3.2). Trade-related and transportation services drove further growth in service exports, while service imports partly rebounded on the back of strong outbound travel demand by local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth.  Chart 3.1: Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions from Major Expenditure Components Chart 3.2: Real Imports and Exports  The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate held steady at 3.4% in the first three quarters before edging down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). Indeed, unemployment rates declined in several major sectors during the second half, including retail, accommodation and food services, partly as the slowdown in the retail sector showed signs of stabilisation. Total employment reached a record high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained broadly stable at around 61%.  Chart 3.3: Unemployment Rate and Total Employment  Real economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. On the external front, global economic and trade growth may continue to be subdued amid uncertainty surrounding the global macroeconomic and financial environment. Furthermore, the rise in the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate driven by US dollar strength is likely to weigh on Hong Kong's export performance. On the domestic front, while stable employment and income conditions should support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately given the drag from rising interest rates. Building and construction activity should grow steadily as housing supply increases and various infrastructure projects are scheduled to commence, although weak business sentiment and rising interest rates may dampen corporate capital expenditure. The government currently forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% for 2017, while the average forecast by private sector analysts stands at 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, with external factors being particularly prominent. Policy uncertainty under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, with potential protectionist trade policies posing headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and general elections in several major European countries could also trigger asset market volatility and affect Hong Kong dollar capital flows. In addition, the normalisation of US interest rates will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices.  Domestic inflation has remained broadly moderate since the second half of 2016, despite some pick-up in sequential momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) stabilised at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 through January of this year (Chart 3.4). The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before easing slightly to 2.4% in January. The pick-up in inflation momentum was mainly attributable to higher prices of traded goods and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, traded goods price inflation turned from negative in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, largely driven by prices of basic food items and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the CCPI rose from the third quarter onward as the pace of decline in private residential rentals narrowed and public housing rents were adjusted upward in September 2016, though this subsequently moderated slightly in January (Chart 3.6).  Chart 3.4: Various Indicators of Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.5: Consumer Price Inflation by Major Components Chart 3.6: CCPI Rental Component and Market Rentals  In the near term, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained given subdued import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures. Imported inflation will remain low as the strength of the Hong Kong dollar partly offsets the recovery in global commodity prices (Chart 3.7). On the domestic side, the output gap is estimated to have remained close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thereby restrain inflation in the services components. Despite a tight labour market, wage growth has been modest in recent quarters, with real per capita wages rising 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before falling 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Against the backdrop of persistent external uncertainty and cautious business sentiment, labour cost increases should remain contained. In addition, retail property rental growth is expected to remain moderate given the weak retail sales performance in recent months. Furthermore, the lagged pass-through effects of earlier softness in private residential rentals will gradually materialise, which should also help ease inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is expected to decline over 2017 as a whole, with the government forecasting an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for the full year, lower than the 2.3% recorded in 2016.  Chart 3.7: Commodity and Import Prices Chart 3.8: Unit Labour Costs and Real Per Capita Wages  The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation in the United States rises faster than expected under the Trump administration, this could lead to a faster-than-anticipated pace of US interest rate increases, potentially pushing up local mortgage rates and adding downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. At the same time, Hong Kong dollar appreciation could continue to dampen import prices while also reducing Hong Kong's attractiveness to inbound visitors. On the upside, if global economic expansion is stronger than expected, this could accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. In addition, the increased statutory minimum wage, which will take effect on 1 May 2017, could provide further upward impetus to inflation, though the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage cost increases are passed through to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank rates rose in tandem with US dollar interbank rates. Partly reflecting improvements in the local economic environment, overall loans continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalisation, uncertainty over the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although the market turbulence triggered by the US presidential election in November caused Asian currencies to fall broadly, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar held steady. However, the interest rate projections released following the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on 13–14 December 2016 fuelled market expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate increases, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened along with other Asian currencies, but began to show signs of weakening as market expectations of a US rate hike in March rose from mid-February onwards. The Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered during the review period (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange Rate and Fund Flow Indicators Chart 4.2 Fund Flow Indicators With the strengthening of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index rose by 4.9% between August and December before stabilising recently (Chart 4.3). The Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index tracked closely the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index, as the impact of the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was modest. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-resident investment in equity and debt securities recorded a net inflow in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and sizeable initial public offering (IPO) activity (Table 4.A). However, resident debt investment recorded a large outflow, driven in part by Hong Kong banks increasing their holdings of US bonds, which more than offset the non-resident investment inflow. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded a net outflow in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds indicated that portfolio investment outflows occurred in the last quarter of 2016, mainly due to the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate increases, which put the local financial market and other Asian markets under pressure (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data suggest that Hong Kong's portfolio investment was subject to inflow pressures in the first quarter of 2017, partly because improved investor optimism about expansionary US fiscal policy contributed to better performance in global financial markets. Chart 4.4 Market Survey on Equity and Bond Fund Flows Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalisation would heighten the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. At the same time, uncertainty surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in EU member states may increase fund flow volatility. In addition, rising demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert inflow pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading exceeded southbound trading in the initial period following the launch of Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment fund flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative during the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained large, rising a further 1.7% in the second half of the year, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the aggregate balance and the outstanding amount of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes combined remained broadly at the elevated level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Within this total, the aggregate balance contracted while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes rose correspondingly, as HK$49 billion worth of Exchange Fund Bills were issued to meet banks' substantial demand for liquidity management purposes. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Hong Kong dollar money supply growth picked up as the local economy gradually strengthened. Growth in the Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As the major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded a faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), driven mainly by increased transaction demand stemming from stronger local economic activity and a pick-up in IPO activity. Analysed by counterpart assets, HKD M3 growth mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks' net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which respectively reflected money creation through credit expansion and net inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in HKD M3 and Its Counterpart Assets On the other hand, foreign currency deposit growth remained mixed. US dollar deposits, after growing by 10.2% in the first half, recorded an even stronger growth of 12.8% in the second half against the backdrop of US dollar strength (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted a further 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits at authorised institutions grew at a faster pace of 6.2% in the second half of 2016, with the full-year growth coming in at 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit Growth Against the backdrop of expectations of US interest rate normalisation, banks' wholesale funding costs rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained low, they edged up partly driven by year-end funding demand and catching up with the rise in US dollar interbank rates. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) rose by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward in tandem with the US dollar yield curve, with the 10-year Hong Kong Government bond yield rising by around 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at end-December. In early 2017, Hong Kong dollar HIBOR generally fell as funding demand subsided, while long-term Hong Kong Government bond yields also dipped slightly in line with US Treasury yields. Banks' average funding cost, as measured by the composite interest rate, remained low, rising only marginally by 6 basis points from seven months earlier to 0.32% in January 2017 (Chart 4.9). With funding costs relatively stable and intensified competition in the mortgage lending business, the average interest rate on new mortgage loans fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 following the rise in HIBOR. Feature 4 discusses the construction of a Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index for monitoring local financial conditions. Driven by stronger local economic activity and rising cross-border financing demand, overall loans grew a further 4.2% in the second half, after growing by 2.2% in the first half (Chart 4.10). As economic growth momentum improved, local loan growth accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong, after declining slightly in the first half, rebounded by 4.6% in the second half, partly reflecting higher year-end financing demand from multinational corporations. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans also recorded a moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually scaled back repayments of foreign currency loans. Overall loans grew moderately by 6.5% for the full year of 2016, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Loans to the financial and business-related enterprises and information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half, partly reflecting strong financing demand driven by the better growth prospects of these sectors. Loans to the construction and property development sector also accelerated in tandem with increased private construction activity. On the other hand, loans to trade financing and the manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade sector declined, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales. Chart 4.11 Growth in Local Loans by Selected Sector Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half, compared with 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal loans) rose by 7.2%, partly reflecting an improved economic environment (Chart 4.11), while residential mortgage loan growth accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting buoyant residential property transactions during the period from July to October. As a result, the ratio of household debt to GDP also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Reflecting deposit growth exceeding loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down from 78.2% at end-June 2016 to 77.1% at year-end (Chart 4.13); meanwhile, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% at year-end, with the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio falling sharply to 63.8% due to strong US dollar deposit growth. The HKMA's Credit Conditions Outlook Survey indicated that loan demand would remain relatively soft in the near term. As the US dollar strengthened, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). The offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a discount to the onshore rate for most of the latter part of 2016, closing at a year-low of 6.98 against the US dollar at end-2016. The offshore renminbi interbank market experienced renewed liquidity tightening pressures in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks' precautionary funding demand ahead of year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks built up liquidity buffers amid worsening market sentiment, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (CNH HIBOR) surged to as high as 61.3% on 6 January 2017. The subsequent rise in offshore renminbi funding costs led to the unwinding of offshore renminbi short positions, pushing the offshore renminbi exchange rate to rebound in early January 2017, with the spread between the offshore and onshore renminbi rates turning to a premium. Since mid-January, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have stabilised somewhat, liquidity conditions have gradually improved, and overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fell to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively at end-February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared to the same period in 2015, driven by growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment charges. The capital position and asset quality of banks also remained sound. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose noticeably following the US interest rate hike in December, liquidity conditions in the banking sector remained favourable. Funding costs for retail banks stayed stable and low, underpinned by a large retail deposit base. Nevertheless, banks should carefully assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US rate increases, particularly the risk of significant capital outflows and their subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. Furthermore, given the continued rise in leverage among non-local corporates, a sharp increase in interest rates could lead to a deterioration in banks' asset quality. To strengthen the resilience of Hong Kong banks against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer requirement will be raised to 1.875% with effect from 1 January 2018.  Retail bank profitability improved, with the return on assets rising from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 (red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profitability was attributable to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment charges. For the full year of 2016, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose from 1.05% for the full year of 2015 to 1.10%. Since retail deposits are the primary source of funding for retail banks, and retail deposit rates remained stable and low even after the rate hike, the composite interest rate — a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks — edged up by only 5 basis points in December 2016 to 0.31%, after having stayed at the low level of around 0.26% for more than a year. This is because they have actively promoted HIBOR-based mortgage loans in recent years, and the rise in rates on such loans may help widen their overall net interest margins. However, the improvement in net interest margins could be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. Indeed, there are signs that some banks have already reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. Over the longer term, as the US continues to raise rates, banks may soon face pressure to increase retail deposit rates, which would raise their funding costs and have a more pronounced impact on net interest margins. Global financial markets experienced renewed turbulence at the start of the year as markets reassessed inflation risks in the United States. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, fully reversing the significant gains recorded at the start of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield rose to a four-year high. The sustained rally in global equity markets over the past two years under conditions of low volatility had been underpinned by market expectations of a continuation of the "Goldilocks" environment of steady economic growth alongside low inflation and interest rates. However, these expectations are now facing risks from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionist sentiment, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while markets continued to function in an orderly manner. Overall lending continued to grow in the second half of 2017, albeit at a more moderate pace. Property price growth and transaction volumes, which had softened modestly in the middle of last year, both picked up again in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, the renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to fluctuations in capital flows to Hong Kong. In view of the uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant against heightened interest rate volatility and potential capital outflow risks. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and the elevated burden of personal debt, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of interest rate increases exceeding current expectations.  Following more than two years during which the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) hovered at low levels, global financial markets experienced renewed turbulence at the start of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index at one point declining by more than 10%, fully reversing the significant gains recorded in early January. Investor sentiment shifted as signs emerged that the global economic recovery could put upward pressure on US wages and prices, which had remained low for an extended period, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate its pace of interest rate increases. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rally in global equity markets over the past two years was built on market expectations of a continuation of the Goldilocks environment.  In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity recovering synchronously across advanced and emerging market economies. Towards year-end, the passage of a tax reform package by the US Congress — encompassing tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and personal tax provisions — fuelled market expectations that the already robust US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the pickup in activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained subdued, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would remain low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets posted significant gains in 2017, with US equity markets in particular reaching successive record highs. However, as the US released stronger-than-expected wage growth data for January, global equity markets began to reassess inflation risks.  Following the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has already reached its potential output level, and the cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts is expected to potentially accelerate the rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy more rapidly. At the same time, as the tax cuts will lead to a rise in fiscal deficits, the US may need to issue greater volumes of Treasury bonds going forward, which is likely to add upward pressure on long-term bond yields at a time when the Federal Reserve continues to press ahead with balance sheet normalisation. Outside the US, strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would result in a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions.  Policy and event risks stemming from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cloud the global economic growth outlook. The US administration appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns about whether trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions could disrupt global trade and amplify volatility in global financial markets. Given these uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook, questions arise as to whether the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets are sustainable. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical increase in global demand and the expected rise in fiscal deficits resulting from US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); moreover, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalisation is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium, which could push up long-term interest rates and thereby weigh on asset market valuations.  In East Asia, regional economies have also been operating in a favourable environment of robust growth and moderate inflation. Buoyed by strong economic performance and an optimistic outlook, capital inflows have accelerated and financial markets have risen simultaneously. However, this favourable outlook faces downside risks from a number of factors: the synchronised monetary policy normalisation by major central banks tightening global liquidity; the US administration's pursuit of inward-looking trade policies; heightened geopolitical tensions; and the potential tightening of offshore US dollar liquidity as US corporates repatriate profits on a large scale under the one-off "deemed repatriation" provision of the US tax reform. Should credit and financial markets face any shocks, capital flow reversals could be triggered, with highly leveraged sectors and economies being the most vulnerable to a tightening of financial conditions.  Regarding Mainland China, the Mainland economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by robust consumption, strong infrastructure spending, and a rebound in industrial expenditure towards year-end. At the same time, signs of the emergence of the "new economy" became increasingly evident, with high value-added sectors such as manufacturing and services demonstrating strong expansion momentum over recent quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist. In particular, the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term growth pressures arising from the further advancement of structural reforms remains to be seen. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to maintain a proactive fiscal policy stance, which may help to cushion any adverse economic developments as necessary.  During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and the containment of systemic risks. In particular, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period following the introduction of tightening measures, most notably in first-tier cities. Meanwhile, as banks tightened their lending standards, banks' exposures to corporates in overcapacity industries remained manageable, while shadow banking activities slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to these positive developments, our analysis suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capacity appear to have tightened, possibly due to reduced support from local governments (see Box 2 on page 28 for details). On the external front, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for much of 2017 as economic conditions stabilised and risks abated.  The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for the full year of 2017, the fastest growth rate in nearly six years. Private consumption remained solid in the second half of 2017, supported by favourable employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices. Overall investment spending also rebounded due to increased corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance improved further, benefiting from better global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net goods exports continued to be a drag on GDP growth, while net service exports made a positive contribution. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018, with private consumption, building and construction activity, and exports continuing to underpin growth. In light of the eventual rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage debt servicing burdens on private consumption. Government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2018 are 3–4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to a number of uncertainties and risks, including those in the external environment mentioned above, Mainland China's economic performance under tightening financial conditions, and developments in the local asset markets.  Despite the unemployment rate falling to 2.9%, its lowest level in nearly 20 years, domestic inflationary pressures remain contained. However, there are signs that quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum has edged up slightly in recent months, with prices of both tradables and services rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up moderately to levels that remain mild, partly reflecting the pass-through effects of rising newly signed private residential rents.  Liquidity conditions tightened due to funding demand from initial public offering (IPO) activities and seasonal liquidity demand, while increased unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions led the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. The Hong Kong dollar weakened again from December 2017 as liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities resumed. In early 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets (particularly equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered.  Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) came under upward pressure between September and December 2017, driven primarily by funding demand from IPO activities and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management towards year-end. In December, the average overnight and three-month HIBOR rose by 14 basis points and 50 basis points, respectively, compared with six months earlier, to 0.25% and 1.26%. HIBOR edged down slightly in early January 2018 before remaining broadly stable, unaffected by the recent correction in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, banks' average new mortgage lending rates still followed the upward trend in short-term HIBOR, rising to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banking funding costs remained generally low after a brief increase in October due to IPO activities, with the composite interest rate standing at 0.38% at end-December.  Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure as US monetary policy continues to normalise; should global financial market sentiment shift sharply, volatility in capital flows may increase. For the full year of 2017, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. Following strong growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half, with growth in local loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong declining across most sectors. Growth in foreign currency loans slowed, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. Hong Kong dollar loans, however, continued to record rapid growth, supported by the favourable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs. As Hong Kong dollar loan growth outpaced deposit growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, climbing to 82.7% at year-end, the highest level since March 2015. By contrast, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 63.1% at year-end due to the relatively slow growth in foreign currency loans.  Both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilisation between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December onwards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool (comprising the total of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit), which had declined slightly in the first half, recovered modestly in the second half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi business, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the amount of renminbi trade settlement handled by Hong Kong banks picked up in the second half. The daily average transaction value of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road Initiative and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The synchronised upswing in global economic activity that began in late 2016 showed no signs of abating. Improving growth prospects continued to propel global equity markets higher throughout 2017 and into early 2018. However, a reassessment of US inflation risks triggered a global equity sell-off and sharp volatility in February, marking the end of the calm conditions that had prevailed in financial markets over the previous two years. Looking ahead, the risk of a tightening in global financial conditions, alongside a range of policy and event risks, continues to cast a shadow over the global outlook. With labour markets tight, US tax cuts could accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to quicken the pace of monetary policy tightening. As the Fed continues to advance its balance sheet normalisation, increased US Treasury issuance to finance the tax cuts could add further upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The spectre of rising trade barriers and the possibility of an unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery.  In East Asia, real economic growth continued to strengthen in the second half of 2017, supported by robust export performance and stable domestic demand. Despite the favourable outlook, the region faces multiple downside risks, including a potentially larger-than-expected tightening in global monetary conditions, inward-looking US trade policies and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialise, they could also amplify the risk of a capital flow reversal. Policymakers face the twin challenges of guarding against risks to growth while limiting the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities.  In Mainland China, economic performance was solid in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made on structural reforms and in containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainty persists, partly depending on the extent to which rapid growth in the "new economy" can offset the near-term growth headwinds from further structural reform. Capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017, as economic conditions stabilised and risks diminished.  As the momentum of cyclical improvement solidified from late 2016, growth accelerated simultaneously across advanced and emerging market economies in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, the United States saw solid gains in investment and exports, supported by improved private sector sentiment and a significant depreciation of the US dollar, while the euro area and Japan recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Emerging market economy exports also benefited from a stabilisation in global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to receive a further boost from cuts to corporate and personal income taxes. In light of the current cyclical upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund projected in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1).  Chart 2.1 Real GDP Growth Forecasts  As growth momentum strengthened in the euro area and Japan, market expectations of a narrowing in global monetary policy divergence, combined with a more optimistic global growth outlook, boosted risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, in turn weighing on the US dollar. Despite three Federal Reserve rate hikes during the year and the commencement of balance sheet normalisation, the US dollar index fell by nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite the broad-based acceleration in growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained subdued and below central bank targets, keeping market expectations of global interest rates anchored at low levels until recently (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to climb through 2017 and into early 2018, with the S&P 500 repeatedly hitting new highs, driving the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio up to 33.8 in January 2018 — its highest level since the dot-com bubble in early 2000.  Chart 2.2 Core Inflation in Major Advanced Economies  However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would lead to wider fiscal deficits and higher inflation pushed US long-term Treasury yields steadily higher, raising questions about whether elevated asset market valuations were sustainable. Following the release of stronger-than-expected US average hourly earnings growth for January 2018, a reassessment of US inflation risks triggered a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 fell by more than 10% from its 26 January peak, fully erasing the significant gains made at the start of the year, and came under further pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protectionist measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply, with the CBOE Volatility Index spiking to a two-year high of 37.3, signalling the end of the prolonged low-volatility environment that had persisted over the previous two years (Chart 2.3).  Chart 2.3 CBOE Volatility Index (VIX)  Looking ahead, beyond the near-term equity market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to US long-term bond yields, and the possibility of monetary policy tightening by other major central banks could all contribute to a tightening in global financial conditions, casting a shadow over the global economic outlook.  First, with regard to US inflation risks, the recently enacted tax reform includes several provisions that are expected to provide a near-term cyclical boost to private consumption and investment. The key measures in the tax reform package include: (1) reductions in corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) a temporary allowance for full expensing of capital investment; and (3) a one-time "deemed repatriation" provision that reduces the incentive for US firms to park overseas profits abroad. While the precise impact of the tax cuts on domestic demand and inflation remains uncertain, given that the US economy is already operating at its potential output, the tax cuts could push US output further above potential, leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. Should inflationary pressures rise by more than expected, it could prompt the Federal Reserve to quicken the pace of monetary policy tightening. Currently, market-implied expectations for the federal funds rate path are more gradual than the Fed's own projections. However, if inflation rebounds unexpectedly, the risk of a sudden repricing of rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4).  Chart 2.4 Federal Funds Rate Projections  Second, given that tax reform could widen the fiscal deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase going forward. As the Fed continues its balance sheet normalisation programme — which is expected to put upward pressure on term premiums — increased Treasury supply could further exacerbate the upward pressure on long-term bond yields. In addition, as market expectations of the likelihood of US tax reform passage increased, US inflation expectations have risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). Consequently, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield, after hovering at low levels for much of 2017, has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased Treasury supply pressures and rising inflation expectations.  Chart 2.5 5-Year, 5-Year Forward Inflation Expectations  Furthermore, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain persistently low as most expect. Although estimates of R* vary, it is widely believed to have declined sharply since the Global Financial Crisis (Chart 2.6). Nonetheless, US R* could face upside risks in the future, as (1) expected increases in the fiscal deficit could reduce national savings, and (2) corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment of capital expenditure could push up investment rates. A rise in R*, combined with expected upward pressure on term premiums from Fed balance sheet normalisation, could signal higher long-term interest rates, creating a headwind for asset market valuations.  Chart 2.6 US R* Estimated Using the Laubach-Williams Model  Third, strengthening growth momentum in the euro area and Japan has raised market expectations that their central banks may scale back monetary easing. Should this materialise, it could signal a synchronised tightening of global financial conditions. In the euro area, broad-based cyclical expansion was recorded across member economies (Chart 2.7). In Japan, the economic recovery also accelerated, with real GDP posting positive growth for the eighth consecutive quarter in Q4 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan have continued to signal the maintenance of accommodative monetary policies amid subdued inflation, the brightening growth outlook for both economies — and the continued tightening of Japan's labour market — has led some market participants to anticipate further tapering of quantitative easing in the near future.  Chart 2.7 Real GDP in Selected Euro Area Member Economies  Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also pose a threat to the nascent global economic and trade recovery. The US government appears to favour inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, as evidenced most recently by the announcement of tariffs on solar panels and washing machines in January 2018, and the announcement of tariffs on steel and aluminium in early March, raising concerns about potential retaliatory measures from trading partners. Meanwhile, negotiations between the United Kingdom and other EU member states on post-Brexit trade arrangements remain ongoing and are surrounded by multiple uncertainties. Should these developments lead to increased trade friction, they could impede global trade flows and reduce global productive efficiency. Furthermore, an unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions — such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political instability in the Middle East, and latent terrorist attack risks — could heighten volatility in global financial markets.  In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, closing out the year on a strong note. Real growth for the full year accelerated to 4.3%, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the primary driver of growth, while domestic demand provided steady support (Chart 2.8). An accelerating recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected Mainland China growth, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted regional exports.  Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic Demand and Exports  Inflationary pressures have remained subdued. In the second half of 2017, headline inflation in East Asia moderated, reflecting a decline in food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remained low across the region, as wage growth was sluggish in a number of economies.
