The positive economic conditions were accompanied by substantial capital inflows, driving significant increases in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (Chart 2.10, blue and pink bars). Capital flows into regional markets rebounded sharply in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations across various regional financial asset classes also rose in line with market gains. Indeed, credit risk spreads narrowed further in the second half of 2017, and benchmark equity indices rose across the region. Regional currencies broadly appreciated against the US dollar.

Supported by buoyant domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. The economic outlook for Hong Kong continues to be subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including monetary policy normalisation by major central banks, stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiment, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, while domestic inflationary pressures should remain moderate, certain upside risks persist.  The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, broadly comparable to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow steadily and remained one of the key drivers of GDP growth. Consumer spending was underpinned by favourable employment and income conditions, sustained optimism in consumer sentiment, and the positive wealth effects from rising asset prices. Although building and construction activity moderated, increased business capital expenditure led to a notable pickup in overall investment spending in the final quarter, following three quarters of broadly stable performance. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth.  Chart 3.1: Growth rates of real GDP and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2: Real imports and exports  Sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. Total employment rose by approximately 0.7% to over 3.85 million during the period, with the most notable gains recorded in the construction sector, the finance and business services sector, and the public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth exceeded employment growth, there were further signs of improvement in labour productivity.  Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from an improved global economic growth outlook and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. On the domestic front, private consumption is projected to sustain its growth, primarily driven by favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Feature 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage debt servicing burdens on private consumption. As for domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activity should grow steadily, supported by increased housing supply and ongoing infrastructure projects. While an improved economic environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, potential interest rate increases could exert some negative impact. The government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3% and 4% in 2018, while international institutions and private sector analysts project growth in the range of 2% to 4%. Nevertheless, Hong Kong's growth prospects remain subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in earlier chapters, Mainland China's economic performance amid tighter financial conditions, and the trajectory of Hong Kong's asset markets.  Domestic inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, though month-on-month inflation momentum showed signs of a slight uptick in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, broadly in line with the average increase of approximately 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the underlying inflation rate measured on a three-month annualised basis, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Both traded goods and services prices increased. The rebound in newly signed private residential rents since mid-2016 may also have contributed to some extent to the pickup in inflation momentum (Chart 3.4). Moreover, labour cost pressures remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5).  Chart 3.3: Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4: CCPI rental component and market rents Chart 3.5: Unit labour costs and per capita wages  Given that global inflation remains modest and domestic cost pressures are stable, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2018, though the underlying inflation rate may gradually recover from its eight-year low of 1.7% recorded in 2017. For instance, inflationary pressures could increase in the second half of 2018 due to the pass-through effects of rising newly signed private residential rents. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation at a moderate 2.2% in 2018, while the government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5%. Despite the benign inflation outlook, upside risks remain. On the external front, stronger-than-expected increases in global inflation or commodity prices could amplify domestic inflation momentum. On the domestic front, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, falling below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a significant further tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation.  Chart 3.6: Unemployment rate  Following the global financial crisis of 2008, interest rates fell to low levels, contributing to an increase in household mortgage debt in Hong Kong. As normalisation of US dollar interest rates proceeds, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow suit, increasing future household mortgage debt servicing burdens and thereby weighing on household consumption. This feature therefore examines the impact of an increased mortgage debt servicing burden on private consumption in Hong Kong.  The mortgage debt servicing burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt service payments (i.e., interest payments plus principal repayments) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage debt servicing burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and the wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices as discussed in standard economic theory, in the presence of a mortgage debt servicing burden, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments and thereby changing household disposable income. This effect is amplified as the outstanding mortgage loan balance increases. Furthermore, principal repayments vary with the outstanding mortgage loan balance, which also affects private consumption through changes in household disposable income.  Chart B3.1: Determinants of private consumption  To measure the impact of the mortgage debt servicing burden on private consumption, we estimate the Outstanding Mortgage Debt Service Ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage liabilities. Unlike existing mortgage debt servicing burden indicators that apply only to newly extended mortgage liabilities, the OMDSR covers all outstanding household mortgage liabilities, which are more closely related to aggregate private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), we measure the OMDSR using the standard annuity formula:  where D_t represents the outstanding residential mortgage loan balance of the banking sector, Y_t represents the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median household income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and r_t and s_t are the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans, respectively.  To assess whether the OMDSR provides a reliable measure of the mortgage debt servicing burden for the household sector as a whole, it is useful to compare it with two commonly used debt servicing burden indicators. Chart B3.2 presents estimates of the OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, along with the median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on quinquennial population censuses. Both ratios exhibited a downward trend in the early 2000s, consistent with the decline in overall household mortgage borrowing following the collapse of the property market bubble in 1997 and the sharp fall in mortgage interest rates over the same period. Despite a significant rise in property prices following the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's (HKMA's) macroprudential measures on bank mortgage lending curbed the build-up of overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the extension of loan maturities for newly extended mortgages also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments.  Chart B3.2: OMDSR and median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income  We also compare the OMDSR with banks' debt servicing ratio, which represents the actual debt-to-income ratio of applicants for newly extended mortgages. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' debt servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only newly extended mortgages but also existing mortgages. Since existing mortgages were originated when property prices were lower, their associated payments are correspondingly lower than those on newly extended mortgages. Consequently, an outstanding mortgage debt servicing burden indicator that covers both existing and newly extended mortgages (i.e., the OMDSR) will be lower than a debt servicing burden indicator based solely on newly extended mortgages (i.e., banks' debt servicing ratio). Furthermore, banks' debt servicing ratio is higher because banks, in compliance with the HKMA's prudential supervisory requirements, include non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the debt servicing ratio. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' debt servicing ratio have remained stable, primarily due to the HKMA's implementation of prudential mortgage lending supervision, including the imposition of caps on banks' debt servicing ratio, which has also helped to stabilise the OMDSR.  Chart B3.3: OMDSR and banks' debt servicing ratio for newly extended mortgages  Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt servicing burden indicators, but offers greater timeliness and reflects the burden of total outstanding mortgage liabilities rather than merely newly extended mortgage liabilities. We therefore believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage debt servicing burden on private consumption.  To assess the impact of the mortgage debt servicing burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the approaches of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real private consumption per household) and its determinants is captured by the error-correction term in the short-run specification. Based on established theoretical and empirical evidence, we include real income (proxied by median household income deflated by the CCPI), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, respectively, both deflated by the CCPI), and the OMDSR as long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total loans continued to grow in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure as monetary policy normalisation in the United States continues. Capital flow volatility may increase if global financial market sentiment shifts sharply. In the second half of 2017, the HKD spot exchange rate against the US dollar (USD) moved within a range of 7.799 to 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The HKD spot exchange rate briefly strengthened and hovered around 7.80 between September and November 2017. This was mainly attributable to tighter liquidity conditions driven by increased funding demand from initial public offering (IPO) activities and banks' cautious liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end, which in turn slowed interest rate arbitrage activities and increased short-covering of HKD positions. As HKD liquidity tightness eased and USD commercial demand picked up towards year-end, the HKD spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets — particularly equity markets — the HKD continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the review period, the HKD weakened against the USD but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate  Chart 4.2 Capital Flow Indicators  The nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) index of the HKD fluctuated modestly in the second half of 2017 but faced greater downward pressure more recently as the USD weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movement of the USD against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate (REER) index, the REER index of the HKD continued to track closely the movement of the NEER index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates  Portfolio investment inflows from non-residents were recorded in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that equity securities investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved regional economic prospects and positive market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-residents' debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the debt investment outflows from residents. A survey of global mutual funds also indicated that both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017 amid optimism about economic prospects and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that equity investment continued to record inflows despite the correction in global financial markets, while bond investment recorded modest outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market Survey on Equity and Bond-related Capital Flows  Looking ahead, as the normalisation of US monetary policy continues, the negative interest rate differential between the HKD and the USD will widen, which may lead to increased arbitrage activities. The possibility that the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered should therefore not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Meanwhile, given uncertainty over the pace of US monetary policy normalisation and the rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, HKD capital flows and exchange rate volatility may increase. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will continue to fully ensure the stability of the HKD exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and continued balance sheet reduction, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and more recently. The HKD monetary base rose further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the aggregate balance plus outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained largely unchanged at around HK$1,226.8 billion during the second half of the year. Within this total, the aggregate balance declined while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totalling HK$80 billion) to meet the strong demand from banks for liquidity management purposes. Entering 2018, the monetary base remained stable despite the equity market correction. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base  Meanwhile, HKD money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, though at a slower pace. Growth in HKD broad money supply (HKD M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. HKD deposits, the major component of HKD M3, edged up 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Among the components, demand deposits grew more rapidly in the second half, partly reflecting buoyant asset markets and increased investment demand. Counterpart analysis showed that HKD M3 growth was supported on one hand by strong growth in HKD loans (Chart 4.6), but was weighed down on the other hand by net HKD outflows from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks' net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Changes in HKD M3 and Its Counterparts  On the other hand, foreign currency deposit growth was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the USD against most major currencies, growth in USD deposits slowed from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits, which had declined continuously for more than two years, rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%. This was mainly driven by a recent rebound in renminbi deposits. Reflecting slower growth in HKD and USD deposits, total deposits at authorised institutions increased modestly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit Growth  Between September and December 2017, increased funding demand from IPO activities and banks' cautious liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end put upward pressure on HKD interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose by 14 basis points and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% in December (based on monthly averages). The negative interest rate differential between one-month to three-month HKD and USD HIBORs narrowed accordingly. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD Interbank Interest Rates  Meanwhile, the HKD yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly in line with movements in the USD yield curve. In the second half, the three-year Hong Kong Government bond yield rose by 63 basis points, closing at 1.52% at end-2017, while the ten-year Hong Kong Government bond yield increased by a smaller 33 basis points, closing at 1.83% at end-2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Interest Rate on New Mortgage Loans  Entering 2018, the HKD interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, HKD HIBORs eased in early January. Subsequently, despite corrections in global and local equity markets, HKD HIBORs remained broadly stable. Overnight and three-month HIBORs stood at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at end-February 2018. At the retail level, while banks' lending rates rose in tandem with the increase in HIBORs, banks' funding costs generally remained low given the still-ample deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage business, banks' average interest rate on new mortgage loans gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly following the rise in the one-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate — a measure of the HKD funding costs of retail banks — briefly rose in October due to increased funding demand from IPO activities, but remained soft for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at end-December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalisation continues and other major economies may embark on interest rate normalisation, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuating global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase capital flow volatility. Nevertheless, the large HKD monetary base can serve as a buffer to help moderate excessive rises in HKD interest rates. In addition, banks' prudent liquidity management and access to discounting through the Discount Window can also help contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate was as high as 10.2% in the first half and slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). Growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed in the second half of 2017. By currency, HKD loans continued to grow rapidly at 9.5% in the second half owing to a favourable local economic environment and relatively low HKD funding costs, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. Among these, growth in USD loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to rising USD funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded robust growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan Growth  Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade finance) slowed from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Loan growth for the construction and property development and investment sectors slowed in the second half, partly due to requirements introduced in June 2017 for banks to strengthen risk management of loans to property developers. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade finance and the transport sector recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans for the wholesale and retail trade sector declined. In contrast, loans to financial and finance-related enterprises continued to grow strongly, partly reflecting the steady expansion of the financial services industry. Chart 4.11 Local Loan Growth by Individual Sector  Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal use loans) accelerated further, rising by 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management clients with financial assets as collateral. The growth of these loans was broadly in line with the continued increase in client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with such collateralised loans are manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidance to banks on risk management of personal loans in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including caps on loan tenors and borrowers' debt-servicing ratios. On the other hand, despite an increase in residential transactions, the loan-to-value ratio on newly approved mortgages declined, and residential mortgage loan growth edged down slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Benefiting mainly from growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. Credit growth, which was strong in the first half of 2017, moderated in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR), the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) funding cost of retail banks remained low, largely due to low retail deposit rates. Nevertheless, banks should be vigilant about the risk of rising interest rate volatility and possible fund outflows amid the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given persistently elevated corporate leverage and high levels of personal debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise by more than expected. To strengthen the banking sector's resilience against systemic risks, the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio for Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 13.6% year-on-year. This was mainly driven by a significant increase in net interest income and a decrease in loan impairment charges, which more than offset a decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets of retail banks edged down slightly from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15% in the second half of 2017. Nonetheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For the full year of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks widened further from 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 (Chart 5.2). Empirical evidence suggests that the improvement in net interest margins is consistent with the rise in the average spread of HKD corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spread of HKD syndicated loans Since September 2017, HIBOR has risen across the board, driven mainly by liquidity demand related to initial public offerings and by banks around year-end, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. In particular, the three-month HIBOR reached a post-financial crisis high of 1.31% at end-December 2017, up 53 basis points from end-June, though it remains low by historical standards (the blue line in Chart 5.4). Into 2018, HIBOR appeared to stabilise as banks' year-end liquidity demands eased. Despite the recent rise in HIBOR, the HKD funding cost of retail banks has remained stable. This was mainly because retail deposit rates remained low during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks, stayed at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up slightly to 0.38% at end-December (the green line in Chart 5.4). A similar pattern was observed for the overall HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, the average HKD and USD non-deposit market funding cost of banks rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding cost increased modestly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total HKD and USD funding cost of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (the red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 HKD and USD funding costs and tenors of licensed banks The increase in HIBOR has exceeded the overall funding cost of the banking sector, which may help improve the spreads on banks' HIBOR-based assets. However, this improvement may be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information suggests that some banks have reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and benchmark rates, or have introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. In a competitive loan market environment, if higher funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could put pressure on banks' net interest margins. The consolidated capital adequacy ratios of locally incorporated authorised institutions remain well above international minimum standards, indicating that Hong Kong's banking sector maintains robust capitalisation. At end-December 2017, the total capital ratio increased from 18.7% at end-June to 19.1% (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.6 Capital of locally incorporated authorised institutions The HKMA recently published a consultation paper to consult on rules for formulating loss-absorbing capacity requirements applicable to authorised institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorised institutions benefits society by reducing the likelihood of financial crises, it inevitably entails costs. Special Feature 5 provides a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment suggests that implementing loss-absorbing capacity requirements will generate a net benefit for the Hong Kong economy. As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirements under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of Category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions edged down slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorised institutions demonstrates that Hong Kong's banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks arising from possible fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce the medium- to long-term funding risks of banks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, Category 1 institutions are required to maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of no less than 100% at all times. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorised institutions, reflecting the maintenance of a stable funding structure in the banking system. At end-December 2017, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorised institutions was broadly unchanged from six months earlier, at 56.2% (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorised institutions The HKD loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions rose from 77.1% at end-June 2017 to 82.7% at end-December (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in HKD loans and advances than in deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 65.5% at end-June 2017 to 63.1% at end-December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the implications of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio for their liquidity management. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. It is estimated that under a shock scenario of a 200-basis-point across-the-board rise in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would amount to 3.45% of their total capital base at end-December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nonetheless, given expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and proceed with balance sheet normalisation, banks should assess the implications of this environment for their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks In the second half of 2017, amid a moderate but still favourable economic environment, the growth rate of total loans and advances of all authorised institutions slowed from the strong 10.2% recorded in the first half to 5.3%. After two years of slowing growth, total loans for the full year of 2017 grew solidly by 16.1%. The asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At end-December 2017, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorised institutions fell to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, compared with 0.84% and 0.61% at end-June. For retail banks, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth of loans used outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks' asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and banks should closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks Strong credit growth is expected to persist as banks have become more optimistic about near-term credit expansion. The HKMA's Credit Conditions Outlook Survey conducted in December 2017 showed that 29% of surveyed authorised institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk in personal lending remained low during the review period. Banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at a low level of 0.03% at end-December 2017.
