On a half-yearly basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to slower growth in personal-use loans (comprising credit card advances and other loans for personal purposes), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong's nominal GDP grew more slowly than personal loans, the ratio of household debt to GDP edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak that began in early 2020 has simultaneously hit both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to arrest the economic impact of the epidemic, financial markets remain volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in both the external and local environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets have continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the stronger side, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable, and total deposits growing moderately, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. Growth in total loans moderated in the second half of 2019 after a mild rebound in the first half. The residential property market softened broadly from mid-2019, though with some fluctuations. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, early signs of stabilisation in global economic growth had emerged, supported by further monetary easing by major central banks, an easing of Sino-US trade tensions, and a reduction in the risk of a no-deal Brexit. However, since late January 2020, the rising number of coronavirus infection cases globally has triggered market concerns and sparked significant volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks posed by the outbreak, several major central banks have cut interest rates sharply and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions have tightened amid rising credit spreads and sharp declines in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will weigh on global economic activity, and the extent of the economic damage will depend on the severity and duration of the epidemic. Over the medium term, tensions between the United States and its major trading partners may re-escalate, and trade negotiations between the United Kingdom and the European Union following Brexit could prove difficult. Weak global demand has continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia.1 Exports from the East Asian region to major destinations including the United States, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported earnings growth, but whether the technology product cycle has broadly bottomed out and rebounded remains to be seen. Financial markets reacted positively to the announcement of the Phase One Sino-US trade deal in December 2019, and the trade truce has to some extent reduced global trade uncertainties. That said, East Asia will continue to face headwinds from weak corporate earnings and elevated private sector leverage. At the same time, the coronavirus outbreak has fuelled concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by a number of economies in the region may dampen Asian tourism, particularly for economies more reliant on tourism service exports. Given the close integration of regional supply chains with Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weakness in both domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade deal with the United States has temporarily reduced external uncertainties facing the mainland economy, downside pressures remain amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and a slowdown in the global economy. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 identified economic stabilisation as a key priority for 2020, alongside a continued focus on managing financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts suggest that mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policy measures to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have noted that private industrial enterprises may have experienced a decline in equity in recent years, viewed as a sign of "private sector retreat." Feature 2 examines the drivers of changes in the equity of mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed company data, and finds that private enterprises or smaller enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or "retreat." Although the analysis identifies negative earnings as the most significant driver, other factors — particularly structural ones — also warrant attention (see Feature 2 for details). Hong Kong's economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year of 2019, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since 2009. A slowdown in domestic demand, in particular a contraction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely dampened consumption activity, weakened the economic outlook, and consequently undermined consumer and business confidence. Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to be subdued as Sino-US trade tensions re-intensified, global economic growth slowed, and inbound tourism to Hong Kong deteriorated sharply. In view of the significant economic headwinds, the government introduced several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks more room to step up support for the local economy and to help cushion the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on 14 October the reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, which could allow banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion for enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the epidemic has recently introduced notable downside risks. As sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food and beverage services, tourism, and transportation have yet to recover from the disruptions caused by social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these industries. Nevertheless, a range of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and businesses — particularly SMEs — including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and specially concessionary low-interest loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme with 100% government guarantee.2 The HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020, which will allow banks greater room to increase support for the local economy, especially sectors and individuals facing greater near-term pressure due to the epidemic. Analysing by GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects near completion. On the external front, the Phase One Sino-US trade deal is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the near term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak could disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to be in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the average projection from international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to a range of uncertainties and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, Sino-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index falling on a year-on-year basis. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social incidents and the coronavirus outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food and beverage services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Feature 3 provides a more detailed discussion of recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, mainly driven by rising fresh pork prices, but momentum gradually eased as economic activity weakened. Inflation is expected to moderate in the near term due to weak economic conditions, consolidation in private residential rents, and mild imported inflation. Market consensus forecasts project overall inflation for 2020 to be in the range of 0.6% to 3.7%, while the government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019, supported by increased Hong Kong dollar demand related to equity activities, including initial public offerings (IPOs). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate further strengthened, partly due to buoyant IPO activity and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tighter liquidity towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner during the review period, without triggering the Convertibility Undertaking. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have been volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activity such as IPOs. Feature 4 examines how market attention on upcoming IPO activity affects the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR). Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020, reflecting banks' continued upward adjustments to their interest rates on time deposits to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the interest rate cap on loans priced at the best lending rate, the average mortgage rate on new loans rose to around 2.6% in October, but edged down slightly to around 2.5% in January 2020 as the best lending rate in the market was reduced from November onwards. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the stronger side, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable, and total deposits growing moderately, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. However, vigilance is needed over the potential impact of any further deterioration of the coronavirus epidemic amid an uncertain external environment. Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to deal with capital outflows and to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. During the review period, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened amid market expectations of a Sino-US trade deal, but faced depreciation pressure from late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In the latter part of 2019, the offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, while the discount briefly widened at end-January 2020, though the spread remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool, after a slight decline in the previous review period, recovered marginally. As of end-January 2020, outstanding renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB637.4 billion. Other renminbi business activities in Hong Kong also expanded, with renminbi bank lending and renminbi trade settlement recording strong growth. The average daily transaction volume of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system for the full year of 2019 remained high at RMB1,133.9 billion. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the mainland capital account, increased allocation to renminbi assets by international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative.

Towards the end of 2019, signs of stabilisation in global economic activity had raised hopes of a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the rising number of coronavirus infection cases worldwide has dashed these recovery hopes, deepened investor concerns over a global economic recession, and triggered a sell-off in global financial markets. In response to the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. In light of the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has cast a shadow over the economic outlook of economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the near term, with the tourism sector being particularly hard hit. At the same time, East Asian economies continue to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and elevated private sector leverage. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weakness in both domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the United States has helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downside pressures remain in the face of the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and the slowdown in global growth, though monetary and fiscal policy responses by the authorities will provide some buffer.  Global economic growth remained subdued in the second half of 2019, weighed down by persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainties, which continued to dampen manufacturing activity and investment. Nevertheless, preliminary signs of stabilisation emerged in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from earlier easing by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as some easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the US-China "Phase One" trade deal. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index  However, since late January 2020, the growing number of coronavirus infection cases worldwide, and the subsequent economic shock, have fuelled market concerns, triggering a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and plays an important role in global supply chains, disruptions to production activity on the Mainland and the resulting drag on its economic growth could generate significant spillover effects with the potential to ripple across the globe (Chart 2.3). Since late February, a surge in coronavirus cases outside Mainland China could exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose the risk of directly weighing on local economic activity.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services from selected major advanced economies to Mainland China in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP)  In response to the potentially severe economic impact of the epidemic, some central banks — including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England — have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. Nevertheless, financial markets continue to face significant selling pressure, leading to a marked tightening of global financial conditions, which could in turn amplify downside pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index for Advanced Economies  Beyond the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. With regard to trade tensions in particular, while policy risks have eased somewhat following the US-China Phase One trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may prove difficult given that many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom are not expected to proceed smoothly, keeping post-Brexit uncertainties in place. In addition, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies.  In East Asia, real economic activity remained subdued in the second half of 2019 amid weak global demand. East Asian economies' exports to major destinations — including the United States, European economies, and Mainland China — remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). While there were early signs that the downward cycle in regional technology goods was bottoming out — including reports from major regional electronics companies of improved earnings at end-2019 6 — whether a meaningful rebound in technology goods exports has materialised remains to be seen. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations  Persistently weak growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital investment declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which could affect the region's potential economic growth over the longer term. To support growth in an environment of modest inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and Korea cut policy rates in the second half of 2019 after having already reduced them in the first half of the year, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation  The coronavirus outbreak has heightened concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid already weak growth. As a number of regional economies have imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism sector has borne the brunt of the impact, particularly for economies that are more reliant on Mainland Chinese visitors and tourism service exports (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and intensifying epidemic would also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese visitors  In the near term, the epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects could prove temporary, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain it. In the meantime, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although markets expect corporate earnings to deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), loose global monetary conditions are encouraging yield-seeking behaviour, pushing asset prices higher without fundamental support. As a result, regional equity markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Consensus earnings forecasts for benchmark equity index constituents  Second, weakness in corporate earnings and economic growth could make it more difficult for private sector entities in the region to service their debts. While lower domestic interest rates can provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds of further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Feature 1, private sector debt overhang risks may also be aggravated as more index-driven funds flow into regional financial markets, though this effect may be limited to companies with stronger financial fundamentals and their longer-term borrowings.  Third, on the external front, East Asian economies may face heightened risks from an increasingly protectionist US trade policy stance. Despite recent progress on the US-China Phase One trade agreement, US-China trade tensions persist, as the underlying trade disputes between the two countries remain unresolved. The rising bilateral trade surpluses that a number of regional economies have built up with the United States (Chart 2.9) suggest that multinational corporations may continue to seek additional supply sources outside China-centric supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine Asian emerging market economies (excluding China) with the United States had risen to approximately USD 167 billion. If trade surpluses with the United States continue to widen, the relevant Asian economies could become the next targets in the trade war — for example, the US government imposed hefty tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.7 Against this backdrop, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain despite the US-China trade truce. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surpluses with the United States  The deepening integration of international financial markets over the past decade has led to a significant increase in global cross-border securities investment flows. A recent study found that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds), but also actively managed funds that reference investment indices.9 By bringing in overseas investors that the relevant economies might otherwise be unable to attract or access, these funds help to develop the financial markets of emerging market economies. In this way, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor bases, contributing to the long-term growth and stability of their markets.  But is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, concerns have been raised that investment by such funds could undermine the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby contributing to elevated corporate leverage levels.10 In addition, some observers argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has amplified the volatility of global securities investment flows, rendering emerging market economies — which are already highly sensitive to global factors and subject to other common influences — even more vulnerable.11 This feature assesses the implications of index-driven investment for financial stability with respect to both of these propositions.  Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to constituent bonds in accordance with the weightings of those bonds within the benchmark index. As a result, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions made by passive bond funds may reduce the incentive for issuers of index-constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors.13 More concerning from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour could encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks for the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies  Using the weightings of emerging market economy corporates within a widely followed index tracking emerging market economy corporate bonds as a proxy for the extent to which their bonds are held by passive bond funds,14 we find that an increase in such investment raises the long-term (but not short-term) leverage ratios of the relevant corporate bond issuers. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 illustrate the estimated effect. In addition to driving the development of the emerging market economy corporate bond market, the expanded long-term bond investor base fostered by passive bond funds also benefits emerging market economy corporates. We also find that the above effect is significant only for corporates with stronger fundamentals — in particular, those with stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios (solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher financial distress costs, highly leveraged or weaker-solvency corporates appear less likely to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment.  Taken together, the above analysis suggests that the growth of passive bond fund investment is unlikely to materially increase solvency risks in the emerging market economy corporate sector.

Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019 due to weakening private consumption, reduced investment expenditure, and poor export performance, entering its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the coronavirus epidemic having recently introduced considerable downside risks. The economic outlook is being clouded by numerous uncertainties and risks, including a slowdown in global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and developments in local social events. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Domestic inflationary pressures are expected to moderate, though the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside.  Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. In year-on-year terms, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the contraction in the second half, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year, worse than the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009.  Figure 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions from major expenditure components  On a quarter-on-quarter comparison, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half of the year (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters respectively, signalling that the economy had entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the main drag on GDP in the third quarter. Social events in Hong Kong severely affected consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract sharply from the third quarter onwards.33 Total investment expenditure remained weak due to heightened economic uncertainty and a deteriorating business sentiment, weighing on GDP in the fourth quarter.34  On the external front, Hong Kong's external trade continued to underperform amid escalating China-US trade tensions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals (Figure 3.2).35 Driven by a sharp contraction in service exports, net exports dragged on GDP in the third quarter, but provided support for GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance.  Figure 3.2 Real imports and exports of goods and services  Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on residents, safeguard employment, and support enterprises — particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and those industries most severely affected, such as retail, food and beverage services, transport, and tourism.36 To give banks more room to step up support for the local economy and help smooth the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on 14 October a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby releasing an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion for businesses, including SMEs.  Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the epidemic having recently introduced considerable downside risks. As some industries had not yet recovered from the disruption caused by the social events, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and businesses — particularly SMEs — including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and preferential low-interest loans with 100% government guarantees under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.37 The HKMA's further reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will give banks more room to step up their support for the local economy, especially for those sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the epidemic.  In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects reach completion. On the external front, the first-phase trade agreement between Mainland China and the US is expected to have a modestly positive short-term impact on the local economy.38 Nevertheless, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow down cross-boundary economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to be in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the average forecast from international and private sector analysts stands at -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding chapters.  The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and in early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among sectors, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food and beverage services industries surged to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social events.39 As economic momentum weakened, overall employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly attributable to the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food and beverage services, and construction industries. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is likely to rise further. The recent developments and near-term outlook for the labour market will be examined in greater detail in Feature 3.  Figure 3.3 Labour market conditions  Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising fresh pork prices; inflationary momentum subsequently eased as economic activity moderated. In year-on-year terms, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) increased by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the rate of increase moderating slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The 3-month-on-3-month annualised rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflationary momentum, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The moderation in inflationary momentum was due to reduced price pressures across a number of CPI components. On tradeable goods, basic food inflation remained noticeable due to rising fresh pork prices, although price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained mild. On services, growth in the CPI rental component trended downward as newly signed private residential rental growth eased (Figure 3.5). Labour cost pressures edged up slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Figure 3.6).  Figure 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Figure 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rentals Figure 3.6 Unit labour costs  Domestic inflationary pressures are expected to moderate in the near term. On the domestic front, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on domestic inflation. With private residential rentals continuing to ease, the housing rental component of inflation should moderate further. On the external front, import inflation is expected to remain mild given weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts for the overall inflation rate in 2020 range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5% and the overall inflation rate at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe-than-expected economic downturn — for instance due to a prolonged coronavirus epidemic — could further dampen inflation. On the other hand, a more severe disruption to fresh pork supply would exert upward pressure on inflation.  Despite the notable slowdown in the local economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8–2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only as social events persisted that the unemployment rate rose more visibly to 3.3% by the end of 2019. With the coronavirus epidemic, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this feature analyses recent developments in the labour market and the near-term outlook, including an examination of why the overall labour market remained broadly resilient during the first three quarters of 2019 (with the unemployment rate barely changing) and what this implies for future developments. The feature also examines some risk factors that could cause the unemployment rate to rise sharply.  It is worth noting that, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. Indeed, the unemployment rate tends to lag real GDP growth in year-on-year terms by around two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why, even as real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter, the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9%.  Figure B3.1 Real GDP growth rate and unemployment rate  On the demand side of the labour market, while China-US trade tensions and local social events dealt a severe blow to employment in trade and retail and tourism-related industries respectively, some major sectors were still able to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the finance, business services, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partially offsetting the decline in employment in trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained resilient, and financial activities in fintech development and new share issuances were buoyant. These factors likely helped support the employment market in the financial and business services sectors. In addition, public administration, social and personal services industries — including education, healthcare, and social work activities — appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis indicates that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, public administration, social and personal services industries respond more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even during an economic slowdown, employment in these industries may not be greatly affected by cyclical forces.  Figure B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019  On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against a rise in the unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors that influenced changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown, the labour force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped keep the unemployment rate in check. However, as the economy contracted significantly in the second half, the decrease in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, while the decline in employment during the recession contributed to a rising unemployment rate, the lower labour force participation rate helped ease the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019.  Figure B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate  Some structural changes in the labour market also merit attention. In particular, the growing proportion of voluntary part-time employees may have helped companies retain staff. Indeed, the shares of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have in recent years declined to 6% and 1% respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group within the total employed population (approximately 7% in 2017).42 As such, companies may be able to retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time staff. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have declined, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours at present, partly reflecting the larger share of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened from October onwards, with upward momentum gaining further traction in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking for the past few months. The strong demand for Hong Kong dollars was partly equity-related and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened towards year-end. Overall, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although uncertainty in the external environment means that market sentiment could be affected by the coronavirus outbreak, potentially leading to greater volatility in capital flows, Hong Kong's substantial foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system provide the capacity to withstand capital outflow pressures without jeopardising local financial stability.  Supported by increased equity-related Hong Kong dollar demand (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar increased further, with the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking from mid-December through to February. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly attributable to buoyant IPO activity and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased somewhat and the Hong Kong dollar softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2).  Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes  The Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the impact on the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) index was limited, with the REER broadly following the movement of the NEER.  Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates  In assessing capital flows in Hong Kong, it is important to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts: (1) Hong Kong dollar capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. Hong Kong dollar capital flows focus on the currency dimension of fund movements and are useful for assessing monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Cross-border capital flows, on the other hand, focus on the geographic movement of funds through Hong Kong's banking system, which is useful for assessing the overall stability of Hong Kong's financial system. The two capital flow concepts require different monitoring indicators.  When monitoring Hong Kong dollar capital flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors were to convert their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets on a large scale, demand for the Hong Kong dollar would naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking level of HK$7.85 per US dollar, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars from banks, causing the Aggregate Balance to decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, and with the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate trading on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking in recent months, no significant outflow from Hong Kong dollars was observed during the review period.  When monitoring cross-border capital flows, total bank deposits in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator. When there are significant capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system, bank deposits must necessarily decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflows.  Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner, suggesting that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on Hong Kong's monetary conditions has remained limited. Nevertheless, the risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak warrant close monitoring. With substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources, and resolve to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability.  Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizable, rising 4.0% since end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As no Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, increased steadily.  Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base  During the review period, the broad Hong Kong dollar monetary aggregates remained broadly stable. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HK$M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, before edging up by 0.2% over the seven-month period since end-June 2019. Counterpart analysis shows that the growth in HK$M3 since end-June mainly reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the Monetary Base (driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (the main component of HK$M3) remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit interest rates.  Chart 4.5 Changes in HK$M3 and Counterparts  Over the seven-month period since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits recording a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits of authorised institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, total broad money supply in Hong Kong also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may be affected by various short-term factors—such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities—the figures should be interpreted with care.  Chart 4.6 Deposits of Authorised Institutions by Currency Chart 4.7 Total Broad Money Supply (M2)  Although monetary conditions remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, the buoyancy of IPO activity in the Hong Kong stock market caused the Hong Kong dollar overnight interbank rate to fluctuate more noticeably in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8).44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) generally rose. Large new share listings exert significant upward pressure on overnight rates, and a focused empirical analysis in Special Feature 4 demonstrates that market attention to future IPO activity also influences the 3-month HIBOR. This occurs when market participants anticipate the future subscription closing dates of large new listings and arrange medium-term funding in advance as part of early preparation.  Chart 4.8 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Interest Rates  As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downward in tandem with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% as of 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). At the same time, the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield fell by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%.  Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and New Mortgage Average Lending Rate  At the retail level, the Composite Interest Rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds of retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks' continued upward adjustments to preferred deposit rates to attract deposit funding, resulting in a rise in the Hong Kong dollar weighted deposit rate. Following the reduction in the US federal funds rate target range at end-October 2019, several retail banks lowered their best lending rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, retail banks' best lending rates currently stand in the range of 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding mortgage lending, for HIBOR-based mortgages, major banks raised the interest rate caps set at the best lending rate, causing the average lending rate on new mortgages in October to rise to approximately 2.63%.45 Following the downward adjustment of best lending rates in the market since November, the average mortgage lending rate edged down slightly to 2.53% in January 2020.  In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity and to support the Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed cut the target range for the federal funds rate by a cumulative 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates follow US dollar interest rates over the longer term, short-term HIBOR may be influenced by local factors that could affect Hong Kong dollar demand, such as local new share listing activity. The Aggregate Balance has declined since April 2018, and HIBOR may have become more sensitive to changes in the supply and demand of Hong Kong dollar funds. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of approximately HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has continued to function in an orderly manner. Should there be a short-term tightening of liquidity, banks can utilise the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA.  In view of the potential escalation of the China-US trade conflict, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). As market expectations of a resumption of China-US trade talks emerged in October, the renminbi depreciation trend reversed, and both offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter, briefly breaking through the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US. However, since late January, both offshore and onshore renminbi have again come under renewed weakening pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, and broadly at a premium in the latter part of 2019. The discount widened briefly at end-January 2020, but the spread remained modest by historical standards.  Chart 4.10 Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates  Despite the volatility in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the 3-month CNH HIBOR continued to hover in the range of 3–4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief bouts of volatility in late August and late November due to MSCI's A-share adjustments, and again at end-January 2020 as the Lunar New Year holiday approached.

Amid heightened uncertainties in both the global and local economic environment, the profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Notwithstanding this, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although the growth rate of total loans moderated in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the review period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratios for all authorised institutions in all currencies and in Hong Kong dollars both increased. However, given that the aggregate balance of the banking system remained stable and deposits were broadly steady, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future trajectory of Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, compared with 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Figure 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.2), retail banks' net interest income continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses at retail banks contributed to the slight decline in profitability. Figure 5.1 Retail bank profitability Figure 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite the US federal funds target rate being cut three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, no significant downward pressure has yet emerged in the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market. On the contrary, influenced by a number of local factors—including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand arising from large initial public offerings, and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions—short-tenor Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, longer-tenor Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR standing at 2.43% at end-2019, close to the level six months earlier (the blue line in Figure 5.3). At the retail level, since Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts. On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for longer-term stable deposit funding. Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate—a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks—rose gradually from 0.95% six months ago to 1.09% at end-2019, though it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (the green line in Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, as the decline in US dollar funding costs of Hong Kong licensed banks offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of Hong Kong licensed banks edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Figure 5.4). Looking ahead, a number of external and domestic downside risk factors will continue to cast a shadow over the earnings outlook for banks. These include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of Sino-US trade relations, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could dampen the already fragile momentum of global economic growth and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the low global interest rate environment is likely to persist, which could exert pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, social events in Hong Kong since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against a backdrop of already weak economic conditions, a continuation or further escalation of these events could worsen the outlook for credit demand and banks' asset quality. On broader market developments, following the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's granting of eight virtual bank licences, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to offer virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by offering more user-friendly products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the near-term impact may still be moderate given the currently limited scale of virtual banks' operations, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to maintain their competitiveness. The results in Box 5 indicate that there is a statistically significant correlation between the degree of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks and improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability. The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. At end-2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions rose further to 20.7% (Figure 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% comprised Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (as measured by the change in total loans and advances of all authorised institutions) recorded a moderate increase of 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 5.12).
