The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines brought hopes of economic reopening and boosted the global growth outlook. Combined with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets repeatedly hit new highs. Nevertheless, the global outlook remained shrouded in uncertainty, and the pace of recovery was expected to vary across economies. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the lasting economic scarring caused by the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers going forward. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, driven mainly by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, partly reflecting subdued economic activity and reduced credit demand amid recurring waves of the pandemic, although modest growth was still recorded for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and continued geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges for Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment capacity of corporates and households, and banks should remain vigilant about the impact of such downside risk factors on asset quality.  Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but slowed again from the fourth quarter as COVID-19 infection numbers resurged. Nonetheless, with vaccine development achieving breakthroughs by end-2020, markets were hopeful that the pandemic would eventually be brought under control, facilitating a return to normalcy and an acceleration of global economic growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, even as signs of disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing measures could lead to inflation overshooting expectations, potentially prompting central banks to reduce monetary easing sooner than anticipated and ending financial markets' expectations of a "lower for longer" monetary policy stance.  Over the longer term, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extended relief measures and address the numerous pandemic-induced economic legacies, including elevated global debt levels and lasting economic scarring.  In East Asia, GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. With risk appetite increasing, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded and search-for-yield activities resumed. Despite these positive developments, East Asia continued to face persistent uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and services sectors. Second, potential variability in vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, combined with a deterioration in government fiscal positions across the region, could dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows.  As for mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumer activity gradually returned to normal. For the full year 2020, the mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will largely depend on pandemic developments and the evolution of China-US tensions. The latest consensus forecasts suggest that the mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi experienced several months of depreciation at the start of 2020, but strengthened for the remainder of the year as economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened, and strong capital inflows into the mainland bond market were recorded. A detailed study showed that fundamental factors, rather than market sentiment, played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate movements during the COVID-19 outbreak (see Feature 1 for details).  The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels. Seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, underpinned by a mild pickup in domestic demand and a further expansion in goods exports, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and marked the first time in history that Hong Kong recorded two consecutive years of contraction, following a 1.2% decline in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry showed that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more sharply than the overall economy amid the pandemic. In response to the continued pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020, providing support to affected industries and residents and enhancing Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to stimulate the economy, including a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100% government-guaranteed personal loan for the unemployed. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October 2021, along with an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers.  With COVID-19 vaccines offering the prospect of a return to normal economic activity, the local economy is expected to return to positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including pandemic developments and the pace and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face considerable challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's goods and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the success of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecast real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% for 2021, while the average growth forecast by international institutions and private sector analysts stands at 4.4%.  Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and into early 2021. The unemployment rate climbed further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced additional targeted measures (such as one-off subsidies) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support sectors hardest hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure given weak economic conditions. Feature 2 examines the potential impact of fluctuations in inbound tourism on the local labour market.  Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation declined significantly on a year-on-year basis to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021, respectively. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, remained at a subdued level in recent months, though with some fluctuation. Given that both global and local economic conditions remain challenging, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures are likely to remain mild in the near term, particularly as local inflation will continue to be restrained by the slowdown in newly signed private residential rental growth. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2021 stands at a moderate 1.4%, while the Government forecast underlying and overall inflation of 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively, for 2021.  The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, driven mainly by equity-related fund demand, including demand from buoyant IPO fundraising activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fundraising activity remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the strong side. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in HK$263.3 billion flowing into Hong Kong dollars. The strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 85 times in total for the full year 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. From a geographic perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. While uncertainties related to pandemic developments, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing China-US tensions may amplify capital flow volatility, Hong Kong's ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system provide the capacity to withstand such fluctuations. As the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking increased the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds of retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.23% at end-February 2021, and as funding costs declined, the average lending rate on new mortgage loans also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. Meanwhile, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%.  As the onshore renminbi (CNY) strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium relative to the onshore renminbi, with the average premium in the fourth quarter of approximately 100 basis points, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit balances rising to RMB826.3 billion as of end-January 2021. As for other renminbi businesses, renminbi bank lending in Hong Kong declined, while renminbi trade settlement increased, and the average daily transaction volume of the renminbi real-time gross settlement system maintained a high level of RMB1,191.5 billion for the full year 2020. Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure provides investors with numerous cross-boundary capital flow channels linking to the mainland, and its offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening up of the mainland capital account, growing international investor demand for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative.  Supported by rising global equity markets and active buying of Hong Kong stocks by mainland investors through Stock Connect, the local stock market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. The rise in global stock markets was attributable to unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies, optimism over positive progress in vaccine development that could help accelerate the recovery of economic activity, and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainty. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses following the sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the review period and briefly surpassing the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021 to reach a 32-month high.  Supported by steady issuance, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. After experiencing substantial net outflows in the first half of 2020, bond fund flows into the local market rebounded as global governments introduced unprecedented economic stimulus measures and market confidence rapidly recovered. Although bond yields saw a moderate rebound during the same period, global bond yields including those in Hong Kong remained near historically low levels.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets anticipated that the COVID-19 pandemic would eventually come to an end and that global economic growth would accelerate thereafter. Combined with expectations of a "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at end-2020, and financial markets rose to new highs at the start of 2021. However, the elevated expectations of financial markets were at odds with the still challenging macroeconomic environment, and there was a risk that asset prices could become volatile if the economic recovery fell short of expectations or if policy support was withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, due to inflation exceeding expectations). Looking ahead, policymakers face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support and must also address the many challenges left in the wake of the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and lasting economic scarring. Continued uncertainty surrounding the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, with less developed emerging market economies in the region potentially facing greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in vaccination rollout could reverse current optimism and destabilise capital flows and financial markets. In Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activity gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains uncertain, depending to a large extent on the trajectory of the pandemic and developments in US-China tensions. Against this backdrop, the authorities announced their intention to maintain a supportive policy stance while emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks.  Buoyed by the purchasing power released by economic reopening, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in Q3 2020. However, since Q4, COVID-19 case numbers rose again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, and global growth momentum weakened once more. Towards end-2020, more transmissible variants of the virus emerged and subsequently spread worldwide, making the situation more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines at end-2020, markets expected the pandemic to eventually come to an end and for the global economy to return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driver underpinning the global economic recovery came from sustained policy stimulus, including commitments by major central banks to maintain "lower for longer" monetary policy amid subdued inflation, as well as continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies — most notably the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) revised upward its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 forecast (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1: IMF real GDP growth forecasts made in January 2021 and October 2020.  Against this backdrop, market optimism intensified, with share prices in cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recoveries rising, driving global equity prices and valuations to new highs at the start of 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2: 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major equity indices.  However, the strong performance of financial markets was accompanied by still challenging macroeconomic conditions, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the outlook for pandemic containment depends on the successful broad distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, overall global vaccination rates remained low (Chart 2.3). Although there are global mechanisms (such as COVAX) to promote more equitable vaccine distribution, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe due to limited vaccine supply. If pandemic control falls short of expectations, governments may need to maintain social distancing and other restrictive measures, thereby dampening the global recovery outlook. Chart 2.3: Share of the population that has received at least one vaccine dose in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021).  Second, the rebound in financial markets is predicated on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, in particular "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn at a faster pace than anticipated. For example, inflation expectations have risen in the United States and Europe, driven by supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and accommodative fiscal policies (Chart 2.4). If inflation turns out to be stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back monetary easing, and above-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4: US and euro area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates.  Third, there is significant uncertainty over the future trajectory of US-China relations. The wave of US-China "decoupling", particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish stance towards Mainland China across both the US Democratic and Republican parties, this trend may not necessarily be reversed under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation in US-China tensions could trigger turmoil in financial markets in the future.  Looking ahead, policymakers will need to grapple with the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic-related support measures. While withdrawing such measures too early could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect", they are costly over the long run, including in terms of fiscal burdens and delays to the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources — for example, keeping "zombie companies" whose business models are no longer viable alive through continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many challenges left in the wake of the pandemic. One such challenge is that global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 as corporate revenues declined and government spending surged (Chart 2.5). Although the problems arising from the rapid increase in debt may not be immediately pressing given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, continued debt accumulation in the public and private sectors could raise concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5: Global debt as a percentage of GDP.  Another lingering challenge concerns the potential long-term economic damage or lasting economic scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty may lead firms to reduce investment, while workers who have suffered prolonged unemployment may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a significant waste of human capital.  In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 following a sharp contraction in Q2 2020 (Chart 2.6). The main driver of the recovery was the rebound in exports, with the demand for electronics and technology equipment being the most buoyant. At the same time, the most severely affected service sectors (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact) continued to struggle. Chart 2.6: East Asia: real GDP growth in 2020.  Despite the continued uncertainties surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment flows have returned to the region. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted stronger bond inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced economy bonds (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production plans were announced, equity inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated in tandem with portfolio inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Currency Index to rebound by around 10% from its trough in March last year. Chart 2.7: East Asia: portfolio investment flows.  East Asia continues to face ongoing uncertainties relating to the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines offers hope for the severely affected service sectors and economies in the region, competition among countries for early batches of vaccines has pushed up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution poses challenges to the logistical and public health capacities of economies in the region. As a result, less advanced economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, as investor optimism has been largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if progress with or the efficacy of vaccination falls significantly short of expectations, the current capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sudden stop in capital inflows could trigger another round of market turbulence.  With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, exports maintained growth, supported by strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical devices and high-tech products) (Chart 2.8). Over the course of 2020, despite the unprecedented shock to the economy from the COVID-19 pandemic, Mainland GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8: Mainland China: contributions of demand components to GDP growth.  Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. However, the sustainability of the economic recovery still depends to some extent on the trajectory of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities on the Mainland have normalised, the services sector is still subject to some disruption following fresh outbreaks of the pandemic in several northern provinces. On the external front, while exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain given the renewed waves of the pandemic in most advanced economies. Furthermore, US-China tensions may not ease in the near term, although the recently concluded Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement and the agreed-in-principle Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the European Union could facilitate further integration between China and other economies, potentially partly offsetting the adverse effects of US-China decoupling on the economic recovery.  Taking into account the continued uncertainties in the economic outlook, the authorities announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that existing policy settings would not change significantly in 2021, in order to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining macro-leverage stability and ensuring the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. In the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan identifies technological self-reliance and the dual circulation strategy as priority development directions, with the aim of bringing per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035.  The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the repayment capacity of bond issuers appeared to be limited, and the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remained low in the second half of 2020. However, the total volume of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 due to a significant rise in defaults by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) (Chart 2.9). While the rise in SOE defaults primarily reflected the central government's determination to break the "rigid repayment" guarantee for SOEs in order to promote more appropriate market-based risk pricing, the constrained fiscal space of some local governments — particularly those in less developed regions — may also have been a contributing factor. Chart 2.9: Mainland China: scale and proportion of onshore bond defaults.  In the second half of 2020, financing costs increased for corporate issuers, particularly for some higher-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and the gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to rising financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default events in the final quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10: Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields.  In the property market, Mainland property prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. By contrast, property price increases in lower-tier cities were much slower (Chart 2.11). The housing oversupply problem that had plagued third-tier cities in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded robust sales amid buoyant market sentiment. As of end-2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio for third-tier cities stood at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months recorded in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels, Hong Kong's economy showed improvement in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in domestic demand and further expansion in merchandise exports. With hopes that COVID-19 vaccination would normalise economic activity, the local economy was expected to return to growth in 2021 following the most severe contraction on record in 2020. Nevertheless, the strength and pace of the economic recovery were subject to considerable uncertainty, depending on the development of the pandemic as well as the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that it would take time for vaccination to become widespread, the local economy would face significant challenges in early 2021. Accordingly, the labour market was expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflationary pressures were expected to stay mild.  Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), although economic activity remained well below pre-outbreak levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter, and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and also marked the first time in history that back-to-back annual contractions were recorded, following the 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP-by-industry data also showed that economic activity in the vast majority of sectors registered year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter comparison, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending a previous streak of five consecutive quarterly declines (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Private consumption expenditure returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, though consumer confidence remained subdued amid the third and fourth waves of local infections, which prompted the authorities to reinstate social distancing measures. Overall investment spending also increased in the second half of the year as business sentiment improved temporarily. Hong Kong's goods trade expanded further (Chart 3.2), partly benefiting from a strengthening in exports, particularly those destined for Mainland China. Services trade remained weak as global tourism stayed largely at a standstill. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) dragged on GDP in the second half, partly reflecting the slower pace of recovery in goods exports compared with imports. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100% government-guaranteed personal loan for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, and also announced an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help ease the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers.  With COVID-19 vaccines offering a prospect of the normalisation of economic activity, Hong Kong's economy is expected to return to positive growth in 2021 as a whole, though the strength and pace of recovery remain subject to significant uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and efficacy of vaccine rollout. Given the time needed for widespread vaccination, the local economy will continue to face considerable challenges in the earlier part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support to Hong Kong's goods and services exports, while the pace of recovery among other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, which will in turn affect Hong Kong's goods trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecast full-year real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021, while the average forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts stood at 4.4%.  Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and into early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed further to 7.2% in February 2021, the highest level in 17 years (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest since the SARS epidemic. Total employment stabilised after falling to a trough (Chart 3.3), while government figures showed a sustained decline in job vacancies. The nominal average wage index for employees, which reflects labour income, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the deteriorating labour market conditions, the Government introduced the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support sectors severely hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure given weak economic conditions. Feature 2 examines the potential impact of fluctuations in inbound tourism on the local labour market.  Chart 3.3  Labour market conditions Chart 3.4  Different measures of consumer price inflation  Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation declined notably to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, showed some fluctuation but also remained at a low level in recent months. Specifically, price pressures for basic food eased, with dining-out costs declining noticeably as more restaurants offered takeaway discounts during periods when dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures for other traded goods (such as consumer durables) remained moderate. On the services side, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remained soft as private residential rents consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures also moderated in recent quarters (Chart 3.6).  Chart 3.5  CPI rental component and market rents Chart 3.6  Unit labour cost  Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong should stay mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation will continue to be restrained by the slowdown in private residential rental growth on newly signed leases. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2021 is a moderate 1.4%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation of 1% and overall inflation of 1.6% for 2021.  As the COVID-19 pandemic took hold, inbound tourism collapsed rapidly, raising concerns about potential scarring effects on the subsequent recovery of the labour market. This feature empirically analyses the impact of tourism booms on Hong Kong's labour market as a means of examining the potential implications of the current tourism downturn.  Inbound tourism to Hong Kong has experienced significant ups and downs since 2000 (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS), commonly known as the "free individual visit" scheme, in July of that year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the original scheme, Mainland residents could apply to visit Hong Kong individually for one to two trips per year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded in April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry Individual Visit permits (permitting multiple visits per year). Mainland visitor numbers increased substantially thereafter. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting Hong Kong with the Mainland, visitor arrivals reached record highs in late 2018 and early 2019. Local social incidents subsequently halved visitor numbers in the second half of 2019, and inbound tourism has been at a virtual standstill since late January 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic.  Chart B2.1  Visitor arrivals and related policies  We use the tourism boom generated by the IVS as a case study to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We consider the IVS launched in 2003 to be akin to a random economic shock, as it was quasi-exogenous in its timing and could not be anticipated by Hong Kong residents. Our primary analysis draws on demographic data from Hong Kong population censuses or by-censuses. Specifically, we use 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 population censuses or by-censuses. We also define tourism-related industries as the food and beverage, retail, hotel and transport sectors.  First, we adopt a difference-in-differences framework to compare the employment outcomes of younger workers (aged 20–40) in the treatment group with those of older workers (aged 41–65) in the comparison group before and after the implementation of the IVS. We assign the younger cohort to the treatment group because they were still at an early stage of their careers and could make more significant adjustments to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the tourism boom generated by the IVS on the labour market may evolve over time, we also employ an event study approach to identify time-varying effects.  Our empirical findings indicate that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers — particularly women and workers with only a secondary level of education — were more likely to enter tourism-related industries following the implementation of the IVS. Notably, the effect of the IVS on the probability of young women being employed in tourism-related industries was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards (in terms of the average difference in entry probability relative to the older cohort) (Chart B2.2).  We also employ a similar approach to compare the earnings of workers in tourism-related industries (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimation results indicate that after the implementation of the IVS, workers in tourism-related industries experienced higher income growth than employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, female workers and lower-educated workers in tourism-related industries saw larger and rising income gains (of 3–20 percentage points) compared with their counterparts in other industries (Chart B2.3).  Chart B2.2  Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3  Impact of the IVS on income of female and lower-educated workers  These findings are broadly consistent with international experience, highlighting that tourism is an important source of employment, particularly for young people, women and workers with lower levels of education. In the context of Hong Kong, our results are also consistent with earlier analyses, pointing to the fact that strong growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of the labour market. As inbound tourism has swung from boom to bust, these groups of workers may be disproportionately affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to trade near the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, which was triggered multiple times during September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related fund flows, including those from buoyant initial public offering (IPO) activities and southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the aggregate balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) fell across the board. Although uncertainties relating to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions in US-China relations could amplify fluctuations in fund flows, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system capable of withstanding pressures arising from such volatility.  The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded near the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related fund flows, including those from buoyant IPO activities and southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some IPO proceeds were subsequently remitted out of Hong Kong, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained in a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, supported by improved sentiment in the local stock market and expectations of increased demand for funds towards year-end. As fund-raising activities continued to be active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly.  During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times, resulting in an increase in the aggregate balance, reflecting substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, causing the aggregate balance to rise from HK$193.1 billion at end-August to HK$457.5 billion at end-February (Chart 4.3). Throughout 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, and there was no sign of any significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any abnormal capital movements.  Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Equity Capital Raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes  During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Index (NEER) broadly declined in tandem with the weakness of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had a limited impact on the Real Effective Exchange Rate Index (REER), the movement of the Hong Kong dollar REER broadly followed that of the NEER.  Chart 4.4 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates  Looking ahead, uncertainties relating to pandemic developments, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing US-China tensions could amplify fluctuations in fund flows. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong sees substantial fund inflows and outflows associated with various fund-raising activities such as IPOs. On the one hand, such activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business purposes. Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system capable of withstanding capital flow volatility without undermining financial stability.  With continued capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base expanded by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the monetary base during this period reflected the rise in the aggregate balance resulting from repeated triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. Other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable.  Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base  During the review period, large-scale IPO activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (HK dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component to rise significantly during July to October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the conclusion of IPO activities and as customers repaid their IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels by end-2020. Entering January 2021, HK dollar M3 increased substantially again, mainly driven by large-scale IPO activities at end-January. Overall, over the seven months since end-June, HK dollar M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the effect of the end-January IPO activities, HK dollar M3 recorded a moderate increase of 9.1%. Based on an analysis of counterpart assets, and excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in HK dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the monetary base driven by the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (Chart 4.7). As the major component of HK dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the effect of the end-January IPO activities, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded a moderate increase of 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined due to low deposit rates, the decline was fully offset by the rapid growth in demand and savings deposits partly driven by investment demand.  Chart 4.6 Deposits with Authorized Institutions by Currency Chart 4.7 HK Dollar M3 and Changes in Counterpart Assets  Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since end-June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits rose strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities, total deposits with authorized institutions rose substantially by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the end-January IPO activities, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics can be volatile due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand as well as business and investment-related activities, and should therefore be interpreted with caution.  As the aggregate balance increased, HIBORs generally remained at extremely low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale IPO activities in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not experience significant fluctuations, owing to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally.  Chart 4.8 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Offered Rates  The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly tracked the movement of the US dollar yield curve, steepening during the review period as short-term bond yields fell and long-term bond yields rose (Chart 4.9). Compared with end-June, the 3-year Hong Kong Government bond yield edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at end-February, while the 10-year Hong Kong Government bond yield rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period.  Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate and Average Interest Rate on New Mortgage Loans  Retail-level Hong Kong dollar interest rates broadly followed the decline in HIBORs. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds of retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June to 0.23% at end-February 2021 (Chart 4.9). As funding costs declined, the average lending rate on new mortgage loans also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the one-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, the best lending rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%.  Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low interest rate environment in the United States, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to remain low, with occasional fluctuations driven by capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffer to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong.  The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from end-May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting more favourable economic prospects in Mainland China relative to the rest of the world as well as the weakness of the US dollar. The announcement by FTSE Russell at end-September of the inclusion of Mainland government bonds in the World Government Bond Index provided further support to renminbi appreciation through increased investment demand. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium over the CNY exchange rate, with an average premium of approximately 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards.  Chart 4.10 Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates  During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity needs towards year-end, it remained below 4% for most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month CNH HIBOR declined in late December, tracking onshore renminbi rates, before rising again in late January, partly due to tightening onshore liquidity and seasonal factors.  Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR Fixings  The offshore renminbi liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to grow in the second half of 2020. Since the fourth quarter, renminbi deposit growth accelerated, partly reflecting renminbi appreciation and the relatively higher interest rates of renminbi compared with other currencies. Compared with end-June 2020, the outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and Certificates of Deposit (CDs) grew at a faster pace, reaching RMB826.3 billion at end-January 2021, representing an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among these, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. On the other hand, the outstanding amount of CDs decreased by 25.0% over the same period.  Chart 4.12 Renminbi Deposits and Certificates of Deposit in Hong Kong  As for other renminbi business, outstanding renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion over the seven months since end-June 2020. Meanwhile, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions processed by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, representing an increase of 16.7% year-on-year. Among these transactions, the increase in remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland was larger than that of remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong has a sizeable renminbi liquidity pool that is sufficient to continue supporting a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. In 2020 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system was RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Against the backdrop of prolonged economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the COVID-19 pandemic, compounded by the effects of a persistently low interest rate environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Notwithstanding this, the banking sector in Hong Kong remained resilient, underpinned by strong capital and liquidity positions. During the period under review, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures to continue supporting the economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, while the rollout of vaccines may fuel hopes of the global pandemic coming under control and economic activities resuming, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties, together with ongoing geopolitical tensions, could weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may undermine the debt-servicing capacity of corporates and households, and banks should remain vigilant about the impact of the associated downside risk factors on their asset quality.  In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), causing a decline in net interest income that more than offset a modest increase in non-interest income, resulting in a fall in profitability. For 2020 as a whole, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, with return on assets declining from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%.  Chart 5.1  Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2  Net interest margin of retail banks  Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more ample largely due to substantial fund inflows driven by stock market activities. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Among them, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at end-2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The Composite Interest Rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds of retail banks) followed a broadly similar trend, declining significantly from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.28% at end-2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the Composite Interest Rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit interest rates by some major retail banks.  Chart 5.3  Interest rates  From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of locally incorporated licensed banks fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4).  Chart 5.4  Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks  Looking ahead, the earnings outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging given that the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist, continuing to weigh on banks' net interest margin performance. In addition, while breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term.  The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained solid and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions stood at 20.7% at end-December 2020, well above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio for the period was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was in the form of Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at end-December 2020, well above the statutory minimum requirement of 3% (Chart 5.6).  Chart 5.5  Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorised institutions Chart 5.6  Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorised institutions  Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the period under review. The average LCR of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%.  Chart 5.7  Liquidity Coverage Ratio  The most recent figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirements also indicate stable funding positions of authorised institutions. The average NSFR of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and stable funding positions of authorised institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks.  Chart 5.8  Net Stable Funding Ratio  Customer deposits remained the primary funding source of authorised institutions, reflecting the maintenance of a stable funding structure in the banking system. At end-2020, customer deposits as a percentage of total liabilities of all authorised institutions hovered around 56.1%, broadly unchanged from the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9).  Chart 5.9  Liability structure of all authorised institutions  As total deposits of all authorised institutions increased while total loans decreased in the second half of 2020, the average loan-to-deposit ratio (LDR) of all authorised institutions in all currencies fell from 76.0% at end-June 2020 to 72.3% at end-2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, the average Hong Kong dollar LDR and foreign currency LDR declined to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively at end-2020, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier.  Chart 5.10  Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorised institutions  Interest rate risk exposures of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. The potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks under a 200-basis-point upward shock to Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates was estimated to be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at end-December 2020 (Chart 5.11).  Chart 5.11  Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks  Against the backdrop of recurrent waves of the pandemic and persistent economic downturn caused by tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances recorded a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for 2020 as a whole, total credit extended by the banking sector still registered positive growth, though the pace slowed markedly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorised institutions, after growing 3.0% in the first half of 2020, fell by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was attributable to decreases in both domestic lending (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Among these, total domestic loans fell slightly by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with increases of 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six-month period.  Chart 5.12  Loan growth  Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans, after declining by 2.0% in the first half, remained broadly unchanged at the end of 2020 compared with the level at end-June. Foreign currency loans, after surging 10.6% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a fall in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved.  Banks' outlook on short-term credit demand turned slightly more optimistic than six months ago. The HKMA's Survey on Credit Conditions Outlook conducted in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed authorised institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the following three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decrease over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A).  As the pandemic continued to adversely affect the debt-servicing capacity of households and corporations, loan quality of banks deteriorated slightly, though it remained sound by historical and international standards. Furthermore, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also moderated in the second half of 2020. The overall classified loan ratio of all authorised institutions rose mildly from 0.79% six months ago to 0.9% at end-2020, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorised institutions rose from 0.49% at end-June 2020 to 0.57% at end-2020. For retail banks, the overall classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, global economic performance remained subdued, while inflationary pressures continued to intensify across the world, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainty, including the risk of large-scale pandemic outbreaks, and the possibility that monetary policy tightening could exceed expectations if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. Should the Federal Reserve tighten monetary policy substantially, leading to a tightening of global financial conditions, this would exert pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could have significant repercussions on the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For the full year of 2021, growth in total bank loans accelerated. Meanwhile, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could pose a threat to the continued economic recovery, and the possibility that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation may be faster than expected presents risk factors that will challenge banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios.  Global economic growth began to slow in late 2021, with weakness extending into 2022, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant led to increased mobility restrictions worldwide and persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. At the same time, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, having already spread to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. More recently, the sharp rise in commodity prices triggered by the Russia-Ukraine military conflict could further aggravate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility could tighten global financial conditions in an undesirable manner, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook.  Looking ahead, there is significant uncertainty surrounding the global economic outlook. In the near term, the possibility of reimposing lockdown measures and a renewed deterioration of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out in the event of large-scale pandemic outbreaks. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected has grown, the Federal Reserve has adopted a more hawkish stance, accelerating the timeline for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussing balance sheet reduction. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financial conditions could also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt-servicing capacity, and disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. The Russia-Ukraine military conflict could also expose global commodity prices to sustained upward pressure, exacerbate industrial goods supply shortages, and heighten financial market volatility. Increased market volatility could also trigger redemption pressure on open-ended funds, raising their liquidity risk. Feature 1 examines whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool.  In Emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the recovery momentum temporarily slowed as some Southeast Asian economies reimposed strict pandemic control measures in the third quarter, while technology-exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from robust global demand for technology products. While broad-based recovery in Emerging Asia is widely anticipated in 2022, the region's near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants of the virus remain a concern, particularly for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and stretched public health resources. Second, the accelerated pace of Fed policy normalisation could trigger capital outflows from the region and exacerbate currency depreciation pressures; for regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. Third, the slowdown in major economies, combined with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the outlook for trade growth. Fourth, the rise in the prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will feed through to regional inflation while simultaneously weighing on consumption. With increased global economic uncertainty, the monetary policy normalisation decisions of regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks of those economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs.  In the longer term, to rebuild sustainable and robust growth models, investors will need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is influenced by the environmental performance of companies.  Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by renewed outbreaks of COVID-19, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, with the property market continuing to languish and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term. As a result, the mainland authorities have placed stabilising growth as the top priority for this year, introducing a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. The total amount of onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises both declined in the second half of 2021. Feature 3 examines whether pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain manageable, as mainland banks—particularly systemically important banks—have limited exposure to developer loans, and non-performing loan ratios are low while provisioning coverage ratios are high.  The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, though at a more moderate pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew modestly, as goods exports and private consumption benefited from continued global economic recovery, improving local labour market conditions, and the government's consumption voucher scheme. In year-on-year terms, economic growth in the second half of 2021 was 5.1%, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, the economy grew by 6.4%, the first full-year positive growth since 2019.  Entering 2022, a new wave of local pandemic outbreaks and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund, and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to shore up the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme were enhanced, with maximum loan amounts increased and application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA and the banking industry also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year option for partial principal repayment, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.  Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue its recovery for the full year of 2022, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The government's promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. Buoyed by government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, global economic recovery and robust corporate earnings drove major global equity markets to continue their broad-based rally in the last quarter of 2021, with the MSCI World Index reaching an all-time high of 3,262 on 4 January 2022. The rapid global spread of variant viruses (Delta and Omicron), coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, led to a notable slowdown in the global economy in the latter part of 2021, with growth momentum remaining subdued as 2022 began. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and had broadened to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Rising inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the Federal Reserve's monetary policy stance, heightening the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could weigh on currently elevated asset valuations and prove unfavourable to emerging markets where recovery remains broadly lagging. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, amplifying some of the aforementioned risks. In Emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant across the region, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with major technology-product-exporting economies in the region continuing to outperform their peers. While the Omicron variant is currently not expected to severely disrupt economic recovery in the region, any uncertainty associated with new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the regional economic outlook. In addition, the normalisation of Federal Reserve policy could trigger corrections in regional asset prices, while a growth slowdown in major economies could drag on the region's goods export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, has driven up commodity prices and increased inflation risks, and on the other hand, will dampen consumption and add to global economic uncertainty, making the monetary policy normalisation decisions of regional central banks more complex. Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by new waves of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressures from cooling property markets and Omicron outbreaks. In light of this, the government has designated stabilising growth as the top priority for this year, with macroeconomic policies providing greater support. Global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to the tightening of mobility restrictions around the world. Furthermore, supply chain issues—such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production materials including semiconductors—continued to weigh on output. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, and a slowdown in mainland China's growth momentum offsetting the expected rebound in growth elsewhere in Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF Real GDP Growth Forecasts While global economic growth slowed, inflationary pressures continued to build during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, particularly the United States, which adopted larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic. Against the backdrop of supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labour shortages, inflationary pressures have broadened to a wide range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). Additionally, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up prices of various commodities, potentially exacerbating already-elevated global inflationary pressures.
