(2) "Advanced Asian economies" include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) "Asian emerging market economies" include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties with greater downside risks, and will hinge on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work and promoting vaccination. Compared to earlier lockdown policies, these less restrictive measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have already shown initial signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, should widespread outbreaks occur, it cannot be ruled out that lockdown measures would be reimposed, leading to a renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Suppliers' Delivery Times Sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to ease gradually, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current period of elevated global inflation more protracted than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia could push up commodity prices, the lagged pass-through of rising production costs to final selling prices, the possibility that earlier sharp increases in global residential property prices could drive subsequent rent increases, upside risks to wage growth from tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation has recorded its largest increases in decades, the Federal Reserve adopted a more hawkish policy stance at the December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer characterising high inflation as "transitory" and doubling the pace of asset purchase tapering from USD15 billion to USD30 billion per month, with a view to ending the asset purchase programme before March 2022, while also beginning discussions on balance sheet reduction. Indeed, recent market pricing suggests the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. By contrast, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs, given the euro area's closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine. Against this backdrop, and given that global debt levels and asset valuations remain elevated following prolonged accommodative policies, if persistent inflationary pressures require the Federal Reserve to tighten policy faster than anticipated, this could worsen debt-servicing capacity for borrowers and trigger financial market volatility. Recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe have escalated, risk aversion in financial markets has risen and signs of US dollar shortages have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency basis swap spreads. In the event of a premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals that are still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Feature 1 examines whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can reduce the liquidity risks of such funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In Emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, though the spread of the Delta variant dampened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, South Korea and Singapore, as the region's major technology-product exporters, continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the uneven recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures in several Emerging Asian economies remained moderate. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index While Asian emerging markets are broadly expected to recover in 2022, the near-term economic outlook in the region faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has been spreading in the region since late 2021, its economic impact has so far been less severe than previous waves of infection; nevertheless, regional economies with still-lagging vaccination rates and more constrained public health resources will continue to face the threat of new variants emerging. Second, Federal Reserve policy normalisation could trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, the risk of a sudden spike in long-term US yields—given their historically high correlation with Asian counterparts (Chart 2.5)—could spill over to long-term bond yields in Emerging Asia, increasing the risk of asset market corrections in the region. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian 10-Year Sovereign Bond Yields and Corresponding US Treasury Yields Third, the outlook for regional goods trade faces uncertainties from a slowdown in major economies and the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, factors that could undermine the region's export growth. Chart 2.6 United States: Imports from Emerging Asia and Real GDP Fourth, although trade and financial linkages between regional economies and Russia and Ukraine are relatively limited, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will feed through to regional inflation while simultaneously dampening consumption. Together with increased global economic uncertainty, this will complicate the monetary policy normalisation decisions of regional central banks. Central banks in regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also served as a reminder of the long-term need for regional economies to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in preparation for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines whether equity market returns are affected by changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is influenced by the environmental performance of companies. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a significant shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, some open-ended funds experienced large outflows (Chart B1.1), placing pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Outflows from Some Open-Ended Funds during the March 2020 Episode In addition to investors' liquidity needs, another possible cause of large outflows was investors exploiting a "first-mover advantage" by redeeming early to avoid bearing the potentially sharp increase in redemption costs under stressed market conditions. To mitigate outflows driven by first-mover advantages, some open-ended funds employ swing pricing—a pricing rule for open-ended funds that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, there has been no empirical evidence as to whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this feature conducts an empirical study to examine whether swing pricing was able to reduce outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby reducing their liquidity risks. In addition, this feature also seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we put forward policy recommendations from a financial stability perspective. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing on redemption costs to them. First-mover advantages are primarily present in open-ended funds that adopt traditional pricing rules, under which the costs of investor subscriptions and redemptions (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio rebalancing) are reflected in open-ended fund prices after transactions are executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first are not required to bear such transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem early, particularly when large redemption costs are anticipated. Consequently, during periods of market stress, first-mover advantages become more pronounced as expected redemption costs rise. This amplifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, driven by sustained growth in goods exports and private consumption, recording positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local outbreak and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures exerted pressure on economic activity in Hong Kong. The overall economy is expected to maintain its recovery on an annual basis in 2022, though the strength and pace will be subject to uncertainties and risks including the epidemic situation and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These headwinds may also affect the labour market outlook following the marked improvement seen in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up slightly in the near term amid rising import prices, weak local rentals and labour costs should help contain overall price pressures.  Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), though the pace of growth moderated compared with the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first positive full-year growth since 2019.  Figure 3.1  Growth rate of real GDP and contributions of major expenditure components  On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity grew modestly by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Figure 3.1). On the domestic front, an improvement in labour market conditions, together with the Government's Consumption Voucher Scheme, drove up private consumption. However, overall investment expenditure fell back in the final quarter following strong rebounds in the preceding two consecutive quarters. On the external front, Hong Kong's goods trade performance remained robust amid continued global economic recovery, while services trade remained weak, partly because inbound tourism remained at a standstill (Figure 3.2). In net terms, external trade was a drag on GDP growth in the third quarter but provided support in the fourth quarter.  Figure 3.2  Import and export volumes  A new wave of local outbreak and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures exerted pressure on economic activity in Hong Kong at the start of 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund, and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022–23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme were enhanced, with the maximum loan amounts raised and the application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to end-October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which also applies to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.  Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue its recovery in 2022 as a whole, though the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting a slowdown in global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and the higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government's push for various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% for 2022, while the average growth forecast from international organisations and private sector analysts stands at 1.6%. Nevertheless, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent epidemic developments, the accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and the Mainland could provide a boost to the local economy.  As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at year-end (Figure 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from the recent trough in February 2021, though it remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures re-emerged amid the new wave of local outbreak. Meanwhile, a decline in online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local outbreak and tightened anti-epidemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over a longer horizon, labour market conditions will depend on the course of the local epidemic situation and the pace of local economic recovery.  Figure 3.3  Labour market conditions  Local inflationary pressures have increased somewhat in recent months but remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Figure 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum, also picked up in recent months. Specifically, prices of dining out and some energy-related items rose at a faster pace amid recovering local demand and rising external prices (Figure 3.5). Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the Composite CPI continued to decline broadly, thereby dampening overall inflationary momentum (Figure 3.6). While real unit labour costs remained weak, they edged up slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average wages (Figure 3.7).  Figure 3.4  Different measures of consumer price inflation Figure 3.5  Hong Kong import prices Figure 3.6  CPI rental component and market rentals Figure 3.7  Unit labour costs  Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-related disruptions to logistics. However, weak rentals and moderate domestic labour cost pressures should help contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2022 is 2.4%, while the Government forecasts overall inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% for 2022.

Against the backdrop of risk-off sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over the normalisation of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate softened during the review period. With ample HKD liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) continued to stay at low levels. Overall, HKD foreign exchange and money market transactions continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Looking ahead, while uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong's ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system are well-positioned to withstand the impact of such volatility. Overall, the HKD remained mostly on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking, with transactions continuing to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner.  Since September 2021, the HKD has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the HKD recorded a mild rebound in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, the currency's appreciation subsequently lost momentum, mainly due to weak net southbound flows through Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the US Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activities continued to provide support for the HKD (Chart 4.3). Total deposits recorded moderate growth during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of abnormal cross-border capital flows.  Chart 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Net Southbound Flows through Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity Capital Raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)  Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the review period, the HKD nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) index remained stable as the renminbi (RMB) appreciated against the HKD (Chart 4.4). Given the narrow inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the HKD real effective exchange rate (REER) index broadly followed the trend of the NEER index.  Chart 4.4 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates  Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, pandemic developments and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, capital outflows from HKD funding — the pace and scale of which will depend on market conditions at the time — under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS) could potentially cause the HKD to weaken and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system capable of withstanding capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability.  During the review period, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative. The HKD monetary base rose by 1.4% over the eight months since end-June 2021, driven mainly by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting the continued issuance of notes to meet sustained demand from banks for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes outstanding increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, with the Aggregate Balance (before discount window operations) declining correspondingly by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued banknotes and coins remained relatively stable.  Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes  Total deposits of Authorized Institutions (AIs) recorded moderate growth of 4.5% over the six months since end-July 2021, while HKD deposits edged up by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may be subject to short-term volatility due to various factors, such as seasonal IPO-related funding needs and business and investment-related activities, and it is therefore advisable to observe longer-term trends. For the full year of 2021, total deposits and HKD deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively.  Chart 4.6 AI Deposits by Currency  Overall, interbank market transactions in Hong Kong continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. With ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBORs continued to stay at low levels despite market concerns over the tightening of US monetary policy (Chart 4.7). HIBORs edged up slightly in December 2021, partly reflecting market expectations of higher funding demand towards year-end. The average lending rate on new mortgage loans rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, the banking system's ample liquidity provides sufficient buffers during large capital market activities or episodes of financial market volatility.  Chart 4.7 HKD and USD Interbank Interest Rates  The offshore RMB (CNH) interbank market continued to function normally during the review period. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, overnight CNH Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (CNH HIBORs) experienced mild volatility in late December 2021, while the three-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8).  Chart 4.8 Overnight and Three-Month CNH HIBOR Fixings  Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. Over the six months since end-July 2021, the outstanding amount of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) grew by 30.3% to reach RMB1,113.5 billion at end-January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Of this, RMB customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in the outstanding amount of CDs. Between end-July 2021 and end-January 2022, transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), representing an increase of 18.3% compared with RMB3,181.0 billion in the same period of the previous year. Hong Kong's sizeable RMB liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of RMB payment and financing transactions. For the full year of 2021, the average daily turnover of the RMB Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system rose from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion.  Chart 4.10 RMB Trade Settlement Remittances  Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the northbound and southbound Stock Connect, Bond Connect and the Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect scheme, the continued opening of the Mainland's capital account, growing international investor demand for RMB-denominated assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area development.  Major global equity markets continued to advance in the fourth quarter of 2021. However, major stock markets have consolidated since January 2022, amid growing concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong stock market remained subdued in the fourth quarter of 2021, dragged mainly by sharp declines in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding Hong Kong's pandemic developments caused the Hang Seng Index (HSI) to fall to a near two-year low at end-February.  Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore RMB bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weakening sentiment in asset markets and a new wave of the pandemic in Hong Kong.  Major global equity markets broadly continued to advance in the final quarter of 2021, propelling the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). Supported by global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings underpinned by government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, global equity markets maintained their upward momentum, although the pandemic remained a key risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, major global equity markets have consolidated since early January 2022, amid growing concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies against a backdrop of sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices, and escalating tensions between Russia and Ukraine.  In contrast, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other major global equity markets towards end-2021. The HSI hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at end-2021, down 14.1% from 2020. At the start of 2022, renewed buying interest from value investors emerged in the Hong Kong stock market, pushing the HSI back up to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding Hong Kong's pandemic developments and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict weighed on the HSI, which fell to a near two-year low of 22,713 points at end-February. Profitability of Hong Kong retail banks declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio rose slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by historical and international standards. Underpinned by solid capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the period under review, the HKMA extended a number of relief measures to further support the economy through the difficult times. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, and together with the risk of a faster-than-expected pace of monetary policy normalisation in the US, these factors will present challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios.  Overall pre-tax operating profits of retail banks fell by 16.1% in the second half of 2021 compared with the same period in 2020. The weak performance was mainly attributable to a decline in both net interest and non-interest income, coupled with an increase in operating expenses. As a result, the return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.1). Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and each of us has a responsibility to play a part in mitigating its impact. To this end, the HKMA has invested considerable effort in advancing Hong Kong's climate objectives and contributing to the enhancement of global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following last year's inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA's 2021 Annual Report, this year we are publishing the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document for the first time. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA's strategies and priorities in strengthening the banking sector's capacity to respond to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and how we fulfill our role as a responsible investor and a sustainable institution.  During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability work across the HKMA's major functions. Readers will find details of our specific measures and work in this report, with the following highlights:  Banks face climate risks in their day-to-day operations. As a banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to enhance banks' capacity to address climate change. In 2022, we developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the supervisory process, and explored how technology could assist banks in assessing the impact of physical risks. Given the growing range of green and sustainable products being offered by banks, we also shared with the industry good practices on how to manage these products appropriately, so as to help banks strengthen their climate risk management capabilities.  The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives on climate risk and sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green taxonomy, which will enhance transparency in financial markets and promote greater consistency in green finance policies. At the international level, we are actively engaged with a number of international organisations to help formulate policies on climate change and assess its implications for financial stability.  Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a particularly challenging year for global bond markets, green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record robust growth of 42%, with total issuance rising to USD 80.5 billion, making Hong Kong the largest hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuance². Issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government and the Hainan Provincial People's Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable capital between the Mainland and international markets.  The thriving green bond market in Hong Kong is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds totalling nearly USD 16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. We also helped the Government achieve two firsts: in May 2022, we assisted in the issuance of the first tranche of Government Green Retail Bonds with a total value of HKD 20 billion, which was at the time the world's largest green retail bond issuance. In addition, we assisted the Government in issuing the first tranche of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. These were the world's first government-issued tokenised green bonds, and the issuance marked a significant milestone in our successful convergence of strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology.  Standards, data and talent are indispensable elements for a well-functioning green finance ecosystem, and can only be developed through the concerted efforts and collaboration of different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works primarily through the Steering Group in collaboration with other relevant government departments, regulatory bodies, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop these elements. In addition to the development of a local green taxonomy mentioned above, the Steering Group has also been promoting skills training in the industry and improving Hong Kong's data resources through the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance established under its auspices. Furthermore, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas, including mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities.  In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund's responsible investment work, in particular by setting a target to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio by 2050. We also enhanced our risk management work to improve the climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns of the Exchange Fund. In addition, to fully capture opportunities that may arise from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment within the Exchange Fund by seeking investment opportunities that support climate transition and mitigation, with a view to enhancing the portfolio's long-term returns. By end-2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had fallen by 43% compared to 2017 levels. Indeed, the Exchange Fund's exposure to high-carbon assets has consistently been lower than that of the broader market. Going forward, we will continue to progress towards our net-zero goal by further integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising ownership rights, sustaining collaboration with stakeholders, and focusing on decarbonisation and transition within the portfolio.  Within the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built on three pillars: environment, employees and social responsibility. In terms of the environment, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and promoting a more environmentally friendly market to the general public; in terms of employees, as a responsible and caring employer, we strive to foster a healthy and inclusive working environment; and in terms of social responsibility, we are dedicated to enhancing financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and giving back to the community.  Compared to the levels recorded when we first began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper usage all achieved double-digit reductions in 2022. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the near term, our goal is to fully eliminate Scope 1 emissions and to reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier, using 2015 as the baseline.  Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained effort and collaboration from all parties. On this important global issue, we recognise the need to lead by example and to work alongside like-minded peers and international organisations. The next section will outline the HKMA's near-term plans and priorities in addressing climate change across its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is an immense challenge, and we are fully committed to meeting that goal. We are confident that, with the collective efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the broader community, we will be able to successfully address the climate challenges that lie ahead.  Eddie Yue Chief Executive

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to drive sustainable development in Hong Kong's financial sector and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable institution. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will work to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the banking regulator, we will endeavour to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the banking sector's "Greenprint" common assessment framework. In addition, the HKMA will support banks in enhancing their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, for example by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress testing as part of the regulator-led regular stress testing exercise for 2023–2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to withstand climate risks under an enhanced stress testing framework, which covers various stress scenarios including extreme climate conditions and adverse economic conditions.  To promote the healthy development of banks in offering green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on sales processes in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic reviews to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial sector's green transition, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and key elements of a local green classification framework.  On market development, to promote Hong Kong as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the scale of green bond issuances under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the scope of the programme to cover sustainability bonds, while attracting more green financing activities to be conducted in Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA will also assist in implementing the Government-funded Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Scheme to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. Furthermore, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology.  On our part, we will continue to collaborate with other government agencies and authorities through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sector topics such as skills training and data, green taxonomies, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as carbon market opportunities. Through the Green Basecamp, the HKMA will join forces with the International Finance Corporation to launch various dedicated programmes in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to assist banks in developing roadmaps to build green finance as a core business. Looking ahead, the Green Basecamp will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand its influence across Asia. The Green Basecamp will also enhance professional capacity building among industry practitioners, facilitate the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead the development of new project initiatives.  As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as part of its commitment to global climate action and implementation of the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, work towards the net-zero target, and fully support global climate action.  As a responsible and sustainable institution, the HKMA cares about its staff as well as the community and the surrounding environment. We have developed a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations, as a commitment to global decarbonisation and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritise carbon emission reduction and encourage staff to give their full support in saving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide further guidance to staff on incorporating sustainability principles into procurement processes. To achieve digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise internal systems and applications to further improve operational efficiency, while minimising potential risks that may arise in the course of digital transformation.

Climate change represents a significant risk to the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to various sustainability and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue fulfilling their critical functions in the financial system and channel more funds towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has placed particular emphasis on building banks' capacity to respond to and manage climate risks, and on accelerating banks' efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas including environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 published principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks, and responded to frequently asked questions to clarify how existing Basel Framework addresses such risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into the supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has maintained ongoing engagement with banks to exchange views on supervisory expectations, progress and challenges in implementing the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the bank examination process, which was communicated to the banking industry in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised SPM module SA-1 "Risk-based Supervisory Approach" and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risks into the risk-based supervisory process. In parallel, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress testing scenarios and assessment framework, drawing on lessons learned from the 2021 pilot exercise. The HKMA also formulated plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into the regulator-led regular stress testing, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector's resilience under severe climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Meanwhile, the HKMA is reviewing the Supervisory Review Process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address the risks associated with climate change and transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a thematic review focusing primarily on banks' development and ongoing management of these products. The HKMA identified a number of good practices during the thematic review and issued a circular in December to share these with the industry, enabling banks to progressively enhance their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and strengthen banks' capacity to manage climate risks. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the BIS Innovation Network to explore how technological solutions can assist in physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering practices, which employ advanced analytics and regtech, supported by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce the manual burden on banks and paper consumption. To enhance transparency in financial markets and promote greater consistency in green finance policies, the HKMA has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. Commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, the green classification framework categorises economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its associated products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has engaged with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore in depth the features and challenges of the framework, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct a consultation on the framework's structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. Recognising the potential risks that climate change may pose to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to enhance current surveillance efforts. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, and incorporates analysis of climate-related risks into its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the scenario design and analysis workstream under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped to further enrich climate scenarios to give central banks and supervisors a clearer understanding of the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022, exploring two key topics: greenwashing behaviour3 in the corporate green bond market, and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures4. The findings of these studies contribute to the formulation of policy and supervisory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared the research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and the HKMA's Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA's Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and promoting the mainstreaming of sustainable finance. Through such engagement, the HKMA helps facilitate international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its implications for financial stability, and draws on the insights gained to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA has stepped up efforts to raise market awareness and participation, put in place the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector's response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government's climate strategy¹. The Steering Group's work is primarily guided by its strategic plan, which sets out six priority areas and five action agendas to strengthen Hong Kong's financial ecosystem and build a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthening climate-related financial risk management to reinforce Hong Kong's position as a global risk management centre; facilitating the flow of climate-related information across all levels to support risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhancing relevant skills among industry practitioners and raising public awareness and knowledge; encouraging product innovation and research measures to channel funds towards green and sustainable projects; capturing opportunities arising from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong as a green finance centre for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. Actions taken to date in advancing Hong Kong's sustainable finance development: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. The Steering Group's current work priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), green taxonomy (see "Establishing a Green Taxonomy Framework to Facilitate Green Capital Flows" in the chapter "Building a Sustainable Financial System" on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group published a preliminary feasibility assessment of Hong Kong's carbon market opportunities in March and will support the development of Hong Kong as a regional carbon trading centre, including the development of an international high-quality voluntary carbon market and capturing opportunities arising from GBA cooperation. In December, the Steering Group announced a collaboration with CDP² to enhance Hong Kong's data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) was developed to facilitate companies' sustainability reporting and to assist financial institutions in collecting and analysing company-level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This represents an important step forward in extending the Steering Group's data work to cover SMEs, an important but previously harder-to-reach segment of the economy. The Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance was established by the Steering Group in July 2021 to coordinate training and policy-making efforts among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions, and to build a resource and data repository. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories covering data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, to help the financial industry and other sectors access data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing Hong Kong's physical risks. To support talent development in the industry, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the "Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme" in December, providing subsidies for practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and skills enhancement. Other measures to promote skills training include the launch of a "Sustainable Finance Internship Programme" to create more internship opportunities for students, and the development of a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the HKMA's "Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners"³. "Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme". The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the HKMA launched the "Green Commercial Banking Alliance"⁴, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutes and innovation and technology providers in the region to develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to realise their full potential in developing green finance as a mainstream core business and to facilitate the financial system's engagement in global climate change-related activities. Its operating model provides financial institutions with a one-stop mutual learning platform to access the knowledge, tools and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; brings together green finance leaders to connect green financial institutions from different emerging markets to facilitate communication and explore frontier issues; and drives the global green finance agenda to unlock endless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five leading global financial institutions⁵ became cornerstone members of the Alliance and work closely with the IFC and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities to facilitate the transition to a green economy. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner⁶ committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure can be found on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone Members, IFC and HKMA Signing Memoranda of Understanding. On another front, the Alliance has held 18 training events and roundtable discussions since March 2021, attracting over 6,000 participants from across the globe, including Asia Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, the Alliance jointly published its first frontier issues research report in June 2022 with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)⁷, entitled "Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulation". The HKMA has continued to promote green and sustainable debt issuance and foster the ecosystem of related professional services locally. The total amount of green and sustainable debt (including bonds and loans) issued in Hong Kong in 2022 reached USD80.5 billion, representing a 42% increase. +42% Green and Sustainable Debt Issuance (USD80.5 billion). To demonstrate the Government's commitment to addressing climate change and to drive green finance and develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the "Government Green Bond Programme" in 2018 and the HKMA assists in managing the related green bond issuance. The Government has issued close to USD16 billion equivalent in green institutional and retail bonds to date, with the proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recycling, energy efficiency and conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the programme, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing the allocation of proceeds raised from the green bonds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable members of the public to participate in Hong Kong's sustainable development through investment and share in the outcomes, the first batch of green retail bonds totalling HKD20 billion were issued in May, receiving enthusiastic public support and becoming the world's largest green retail bond issuance at the time. The issuance also broadened the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong, consolidating Hong Kong's position as the premier green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular green institutional bond issuance in the 2022-23 financial year and issued USD5.75 billion equivalent in green bonds in January 2023. The tri-currency issuance covered US dollars, euros and renminbi, with maturities ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to provide important benchmarks for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was well received by global investors and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government's previous green bond issuances, reflecting investors' confidence in Hong Kong's long-term credit standing and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi-denominated bonds to RMB10 billion. The proportion of international investors and Mainland investors participating through the Southbound Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong's role as the premier offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its position as an international financial centre. The HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing tokenised green bonds for institutional investors in February 2023, to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. These are among the world's first tokenised green bonds issued by a government. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network, and subsequent processes (including coupon payments, secondary market transaction settlement and redemption at maturity) were also digitised. The experience gained from this government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) to publish annual reports on Hong Kong's and the region's green debt markets respectively. The ICMA report indicates that Hong Kong became the largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances in Asia in 2022, with a total of USD27.8 billion in bonds arranged through Hong Kong, accounting for over one-third of the regional total. Largest Hub for Arranging International Green and Sustainable Bond Issuances in Asia: USD27.8 billion. Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government re-issued RMB5 billion in offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion in green and blue bonds⁸. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People's Government made its debut issuance of RMB5 billion in offshore bonds in Hong Kong, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again highlight Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable capital between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring position as the premier fundraising platform in the region. The HKMA continues to promote and implement the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme" launched in 2021, and uses the scheme to attract more relevant professional service providers (including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external review organisations) to establish and expand their businesses in Hong Kong. The scheme has been well received by the industry. As of the end of 2022, the scheme had covered external review service expenditure for over 180 green and sustainable debt instrument issuances on a pre-issuance, post-issuance or both basis, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March onwards, the scheme was optimised to lower the minimum loan threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HKD200 million to HKD100 million, helping smaller enterprises access green financing. Following the successful proof of concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitising carbon forwards (also known as Mitigation Outcome Interests, or MOIs) with the aim of enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental integrity of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes to track, deliver and transfer digitised MOIs using blockchain and other relevant technologies.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in advancing green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having led the way in investing in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership published by the Securities and Futures Commission, and incorporating environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "preservation of capital first, long-term appreciation second", and believes that placing emphasis on ESG factors can unlock long-term sustainable value from investments and mitigate associated risks. In the face of increasingly severe climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a "Net Zero by 2050" target in 2022 and refining its risk management strategies to enhance the resilience of the portfolio, thereby achieving better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable financial ecosystem, working with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organisations to develop ESG investment standards. Transparency in climate-related information plays a critical role in managing climate risks. To fulfil its commitment to supporting the Glasgow Declaration published by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 UN Climate Change Conference and to greening the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board.  a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures  The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee (EFAC), chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office (EFIO) in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is to enable the HKMA to give priority to ESG investments whose risk-adjusted long-term returns are comparable to those of other investments, thereby upholding the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA's responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA's website.  The Investment Committee under EFAC, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG and climate-related risks associated with Exchange Fund investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management guidelines, and monitors the progress of ESG integration and the ESG profile of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Monitoring Division of the EFIO.  As shown in Chart 1, the ESG Committee established within the EFIO, chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and overseeing ESG-related work across the EFIO. Motions discussed and work progress at each ESG Committee meeting are reported to the Chief Executive of the EFIO.  Responsible Investment Monitoring and Governance Structure  The dedicated team in the Risk Management and Monitoring Division works closely with the various investment teams within the EFIO on ESG integration, and assists senior management of the EFIO in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across investment portfolios:  Public Market Investments — The Credit, Compliance and Monitoring Committee, composed of senior management of the EFIO, monitors the ESG profile of the fixed income portfolio through regular reports from the Risk Management and Monitoring Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Monitoring Division participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for the equity portfolio (see the section "Striving for Active Ownership" under "Risk Management" on page 27).  Private Market Investments — The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Monitoring Division and the private market investment team on each investment proposal.  Concrete evidence² continues to demonstrate the significant impacts of climate change and related risks. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming full implementation of the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) announced by all regions, it is estimated that global temperatures could still rise by as much as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement's goal of keeping the increase in global average temperatures to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Should regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to narrow the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and market repricing of assets based on anticipated future trends, combined with inherent physical risks, would intensify pressure on asset valuations.  In light of updates to the global warming trajectory and model assumptions, the HKMA, drawing on the expertise of external advisers, assessed the resilience of the Exchange Fund "Investment Portfolio" under the "Disorderly Transition" scenario (Chart 2) — extending beyond the scenarios assessed in 2021. The "Disorderly Transition" scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors in the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets are subject to sudden divestment to maintain average temperature rises within 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2100. This scenario broadly aligns with the disorderly scenario recommended by NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments.  The "Investment Portfolio" is able to maintain resilience over the medium to long term, as a relatively larger proportion of its asset allocation is in sovereign bonds, which are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sectoral distribution is key. Low-carbon electricity and renewable energy assets can benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may exert short-term impacts on performance, particularly for equity assets. The "Investment Portfolio" as a whole will be increasingly affected by physical risks that gradually manifest over time. Energy and conventional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors.  Climate scenarios, like other modelling approaches, have their limitations. The analysis is based on the sectoral distribution of market benchmarks at the strategic asset allocation level, and does not take into account the effects of active security selection within any given sector. Deeper analysis reveals that investments within the "Investment Portfolio" are generally more resilient to transition shocks or less adversely affected compared to the market benchmarks of the strategic asset allocation. This finding reaffirms that the HKMA's responsible investment approach, with a focus on combating climate change, enhances portfolio resilience.  The climate change trajectory remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will periodically review relevant scenarios and refine assessments to better determine the Exchange Fund's resilience to climate change.  As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully appreciates the risks and opportunities that climate change can bring. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and capturing opportunities related to climate transition, climate risk mitigation and enhancing long-term portfolio returns. In 2022, the HKMA continued its positive momentum, increasing its holdings of green, social and sustainable bonds by a further 50%. In terms of equity investments, the HKMA invested in an actively managed equity portfolio with a governance theme, and adopted a decarbonisation strategy for the passive equity portfolio that tilts towards lower-carbon-emitting companies. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with general partners of the Exchange Fund's "Long-Term Growth Portfolio" the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Chart 3).  Chart 3: Continued Implementation of Measures to Increase ESG Investments  The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator which, in addition to generating clean energy, places great emphasis on social and biodiversity factors. Prior to the establishment of the wind farms, local villagers used poison baits to prevent predators from preying on their livestock, but this inadvertently threatened certain vulture species that are classified as endangered. As livestock represents an important asset for local villagers, to help them protect their livestock, the operator constructed livestock shelters within the wind farm sites to protect livestock from natural predators. In addition, the operator employs bird monitoring teams to issue warnings when vultures are attracted to animal carcasses accidentally left behind by predators, so that wind turbines can be shut down to prevent vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win outcome: it safeguards the livelihoods of villagers while reducing vulture fatalities caused by wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species.  Good ESG practices can generate more business opportunities and open up revenue streams for companies, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operations. The investee company is a Chinese integrated logistics and warehousing operator specialising in cold chain pharmaceutical, chemical and high-end consumer goods logistics services. The company faces continuously rising ESG operational standards, primarily from multinational corporate clients requiring their service providers to meet high decarbonisation targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to these requirements, the company engaged external consultants to help develop a "Three-Year ESG Plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030 or earlier. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan already delivered significant results in 2021 alone. The aforementioned ESG measures earned the company a "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. These results and recognitions have enabled the company to win considerable business opportunities from multinational clients in the consumer and chemical products sectors that place particular emphasis on ESG practices.  The growth of ESG investments is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable financial ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry skills. In 2022, the HKMA successfully hosted its 4th Annual ESG Workshop, exchanging good ESG practices with nine participating private market institutions (including general partners, limited partners and corporates), and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. On the public markets front, the HKMA encouraged trading partners (primarily investment banks) to expand their ESG headcount and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong.  Mr Lee Tat-chi, Chief Executive of the EFIO, delivered the opening remarks at the 2022 HKMA ESG Workshop.  At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in developing industry ESG investment standards and practices:  As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participates in collaborative engagement actions coordinated by PRI to develop standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaires⁵˒⁶ for private equity and venture capital investments, helping private market investors conduct ESG assessments of general partners and investment proposals.  The HKMA participates in multiple working groups to support FCLTGlobal's research, which aims to explore leading market practices for long-term portfolios and decarbonising private assets, as well as the application of such practices for long-term investors.  As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS's "Climate-Related Financial Disclosures for Central Banks" guidance, demonstrating the HKMA's commitment to adopting good ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a working group under the NGFS "Central Bank Net Zero" workstream, participating in the development of sustainable and responsible investment guidelines for the central banking community.  The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars, sharing insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies.  Ms Daisy Lau, Chief Risk Officer of the EFIO (centre), speaking at an ESG Investment Opportunities Sharing Session.  Building internal capacity is essential for continuing to advance the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to pursue relevant sustainability courses and professional qualifications, the HKMA has drawn on knowledge and practical experience gained through engaging external advisers since 2021 to provide recommendations on leading industry practices for climate transition in the portfolio. Furthermore, the HKMA utilises ESG data compiled by reputable external data providers to supplement its ongoing portfolio analysis, helping to consolidate the ESG resilience of the Exchange Fund.

The HKMA is committed to reducing its corporate carbon footprint with the aim of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, thereby contributing to Hong Kong's overall climate goals. Alongside its efforts to promote environmental sustainability, the HKMA upholds its commitment to staff well-being, financial inclusion, and social responsibility. The HKMA is dedicated to conducting its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA practises its sustainability philosophy under three pillars: environment, staff, and social responsibility (Diagram 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee (CSRSC) leads the HKMA in formulating and implementing its sustainability strategy. The Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA and its members include three Deputy Chief Executives as well as representatives from the Risk Management and Compliance Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department. The Committee reports regularly to the Governance Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the Committee's leadership, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing measures within their respective areas. In 2022, the CSRSC approved the climate targets for corporate operations and reviewed the transition roadmap for achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. During the year, the Committee continued to review the progress of the HKMA's green measures, including proposals to strengthen its sustainable procurement policy, procedures, and approaches.  Sustainability Governance Framework and the HKMA's Corporate Sustainability Journey  In recognition of the HKMA's commitment to caring for the environment, staff, and the community at large, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service (HKCSS) awarded the HKMA the "Caring Organisation Logo — 15 Years+" for the 16th consecutive year.  The HKMA attaches great importance to its corporate carbon footprint and has established internal Green Office Guidelines to manage the environmental impact of its operational processes. The HKMA has incorporated environmental considerations into the interior design, operation, and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, the HKMA received a BEAM Plus Interiors Gold certification for certain renovated office areas. This is the second green building certification received, following the LEED Gold certification obtained in 2021.  BEAM Plus Interiors Version 1.0 Gold Award  The HKMA has implemented a range of energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption in 2022 was 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per capita), representing a 24.4% decrease from 2015 (Figure 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in 2022 amounted to 2,996.4 tonnes of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per capita), representing a 38.2% reduction from 2015 (Figure 2).  Figure 1 Figure 2: GHG Emissions Intensity (Scope 1 and 2)  The HKMA encourages paperless operations internally. In addition, a print management system has been implemented, requiring staff to log in to printers to confirm each print job, thereby reducing unnecessary printouts and toner usage. Where printing is genuinely necessary, double-sided and black-and-white printing are encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to implement an internal electronic records management system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per capita), representing a 65.3% reduction from 2015 (Figure A).  Figure A: Paper Consumption Intensity  The HKMA's waste management efforts continue to follow the "4R" principles. In addition to conventional waste, the HKMA reduces electronic waste by adopting technological solutions such as server virtualisation and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external company for the first time to conduct a waste audit to analyse the composition of waste generated in its offices. The audit found that food waste constitutes a significant proportion of total waste, prompting the HKMA to launch a food waste recycling programme (see "Enhancing Waste Management" on page 41). Total non-hazardous waste generated in 2022 (including general waste and recyclables) was 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per capita), representing a 4.8% reduction from 2015 (Figure 3). The fluctuating trend was primarily due to work-from-home arrangements during COVID-19 peaks and the resumption of office operations following the fifth wave of the pandemic.  Figure 3: Non-Hazardous Waste Intensity  The HKMA prioritises waste reduction at source and is committed to reducing, reusing, and recycling.
